cases.title: Design a metrics and logging service.

source_question.title: Design a metrics and logging service.

cases.customer_scenario: A multi-tenant SaaS platform operates thousands of services across Kubernetes, virtual machines, and two cloud regions. Application teams need near-real-time dashboards and alerts, while incident responders need to search structured logs and correlate them with metrics by tenant, service, region, deployment, and trace ID. The platform team wants a managed, OpenTelemetry-compatible service with explicit retention tiers, tenant isolation, ingestion controls, and predictable cost.
discovery_questions: Which signals are in scope for the first release: metrics, logs, traces, audit events, or only metrics and logs?
What are the expected average and peak ingestion rates in samples or bytes per second, and how bursty are producers?
What freshness targets apply to dashboard queries and alerts, and what query latency is acceptable for recent versus archived data?
How long must each signal be retained, and are retention, residency, or deletion requirements different by tenant?
Which dimensions are essential for metrics, and what limits can we place on label cardinality and log field size?
Do customers require PromQL, SQL/KQL-style log search, saved dashboards, and cross-signal correlation by trace ID?
What availability and durability targets apply to ingestion, querying, and alert evaluation during a regional failure?
Who can read, write, export, or administer each tenant's telemetry, and which actions require an immutable audit trail?
functional_requirements: Accept batched metrics and structured logs through authenticated, versioned ingestion endpoints and OpenTelemetry collectors.
Validate, normalize, enrich, and route telemetry by tenant, signal type, retention class, and region.
Support time-range metric queries with aggregation and log queries with filters, full-text search, and trace-ID correlation.
Create dashboards and evaluate threshold, absence, and windowed alert rules with notification routing.
Expose ingestion health, rejected-record reasons, usage, retention, and estimated cost per tenant.
Allow administrators to configure quotas, sampling, redaction, retention, and export policies without redeploying producers.
non_functional_requirements: Scale horizontally to sustained multi-million-event-per-second ingestion while absorbing short producer bursts through durable buffering.
Acknowledge accepted telemetry only after durable handoff; target no acknowledged-data loss within the regional durability boundary.
Make new telemetry queryable within 30 seconds at p99 and evaluate critical metric alerts within 60 seconds.
Return common recent-window dashboard queries within 2 seconds at p95 and bounded ad hoc log queries within 10 seconds at p95.
Provide at least 99.9% monthly availability for ingestion and query APIs, with degraded local buffering during a regional dependency failure.
Enforce tenant isolation, encryption in transit and at rest, least-privilege access, private connectivity, and auditable control-plane changes.
Keep cost proportional to retained bytes and query work by using aggregation, sampling, tiered storage, and per-tenant budgets.

core_entities.name: Tenant
core_entities.purpose: Owns identities, quotas, encryption and residency policy, retention defaults, and billing attribution.

core_entities.name: TelemetryEnvelope
core_entities.purpose: Carries tenant, signal type, event and ingest timestamps, schema version, source, payload, and idempotency metadata.

core_entities.name: MetricSeries
core_entities.purpose: Identifies a metric by name plus a normalized label set and stores timestamped numeric samples.

core_entities.name: LogRecord
core_entities.purpose: Stores severity, body, structured attributes, resource metadata, and optional trace and span identifiers.

core_entities.name: DataCollectionPolicy
core_entities.purpose: Defines validation, filtering, redaction, sampling, transformation, routing, and retention for incoming telemetry.

core_entities.name: AlertRule
core_entities.purpose: Defines a query or metric condition, evaluation window, severity, suppression behavior, and notification destinations.

core_entities.name: Dashboard
core_entities.purpose: Persists tenant-scoped visualizations and parameterized queries.

api_interface.purpose: Ingest a compressed batch of metric samples with an idempotency key and return per-batch acceptance counts.
Ingest structured log batches and return accepted, rejected, and throttled record counts.
Run a tenant-scoped range or instant metric query with aggregation and label filters.
Run a bounded log search with time range, predicates, text search, cursor, and result limit.
Create or replace a versioned alert rule with explicit evaluation and notification settings.
Create or replace tenant collection, transformation, sampling, and retention policy.
Report accepted bytes, rejected records, active series, query work, and retention usage.

component_flow: 1. Instrumented services and host agents emit OpenTelemetry-compatible metric and log batches to a nearby collector, which buffers briefly and applies backpressure.
2. A global or regional gateway authenticates the workload identity, resolves the tenant, enforces request and byte quotas, and assigns an ingest timestamp and batch ID.
3. Stateless validators reject malformed or oversized records, normalize resource attributes, redact configured fields, and apply collection policy before acknowledging the producer.
4. Accepted envelopes are partitioned by tenant and signal and appended to a replicated durable stream; the gateway acknowledges only after the stream confirms the write.
5. Independent stream processors deduplicate retried batches, calculate metric rollups, build inverted log indexes, and route raw data to hot stores and immutable object storage.
6. A time-series store serves recent metric ranges, while a log index and columnar store serve recent structured searches; cold queries scan compacted object-store segments asynchronously.

7. The query gateway authorizes tenant scope, plans and fans out bounded queries to relevant shards, merges partial results, caches common dashboard windows, and returns a cursor for large log result sets.
8. Alert evaluators read the same metric and log query layers on scheduled windows, persist evaluation state, deduplicate state transitions, and publish notifications through retrying connectors.
9. The service measures its own lag, rejection rate, active-series count, index health, query saturation, and alert delay in a separate failure domain.
tradeoffs: Separate metric and log stores optimize each access pattern but add routing, correlation, and operational complexity; one universal store simplifies the platform but usually compromises cost or latency for one signal.

Synchronous durable acknowledgment reduces loss ambiguity but increases ingestion latency; asynchronous client acknowledgment is faster but requires explicit loss semantics and stronger local buffering.
Aggressive sampling, pre-aggregation, and label limits control cost and cardinality, but can remove rare-event detail needed during incidents.
A shared multi-tenant cluster improves utilization and economics, while dedicated shards improve isolation and noisy-neighbor control at higher cost.
Long hot retention accelerates investigations but is expensive; hot, warm, and cold tiers reduce cost at the expense of slower historical queries.
Exactly-once ingestion is costly and misleading across the entire pipeline; at-least-once durable transport plus batch deduplication gives practical correctness with bounded duplicate risk.
failure_security_challenges: A collector or network partition can outlive its local disk buffer; expose dropped-byte counters, use bounded persistent queues, and document whether producers block, sample, or drop under pressure.
A cardinality explosion can exhaust metric indexes; enforce per-tenant active-series budgets, reject or aggregate offending labels, and surface the exact policy decision.
Poison or oversized log batches can stall a partition; validate before the durable stream, isolate bad records, and quarantine rather than retrying the whole batch forever.
Clock skew and late data can corrupt windows; retain both event and ingest time, define lateness bounds, and allow alert evaluators to use explicit watermark semantics.
A hot shard or noisy tenant can dominate ingestion and queries; use tenant-aware partitioning, admission control, fair scheduling, and workload-specific query budgets.
Logs can contain secrets or personal data; apply source-side minimization and ingestion-time redaction, restrict raw-field access, encrypt data, and audit reads and exports.
An alert evaluator or notification provider can fail after a state transition; persist alert state and an outbox event, retry idempotently, and suppress duplicate pages with a stable incident key.

A regional outage can split ingestion from query state; pin tenant writes to a home region or define conflict-free failover, replicate durable data asynchronously, and publish clear RPO and RTO semantics.

deep_dives.title: Partitioning, cardinality, and the write path
deep_dives.details: Partition the durable stream by a stable hash of tenant and series or source so writes scale horizontally without allowing one large tenant to monopolize every shard. Maintain an approximate per-tenant active-series counter and reject, aggregate, or sample new label combinations beyond policy. Give each batch a producer ID and monotonic sequence or idempotency key; keep a bounded deduplication window in stream processors rather than promising global exactly-once delivery.

deep_dives.title: Storage and query planning
deep_dives.details: Store raw immutable telemetry in object storage for replay, recent metric samples and rollups in a time-series engine, and recent logs in a columnar store with selective indexes. The query planner first applies tenant and time predicates, consults shard and segment metadata, pushes down filters and aggregation, caps scanned bytes, then merges partial results. Cache only authorization-safe, tenant-qualified queries and return asynchronous job handles for cold scans.

deep_dives.title: Alert correctness
deep_dives.details: Treat alerting as a state machine over evaluation windows rather than a stateless query. Persist pending, firing, and resolved state with the rule version and last evaluated watermark. Use consecutive-window or burn-rate conditions to reduce noise, represent missing data explicitly, and publish transitions through an outbox so notification retries cannot lose or multiply incidents.

deep_dives.title: Security, governance, and cost
deep_dives.details: Use workload identity rather than long-lived ingestion keys where possible, tenant-scoped RBAC for queries, private endpoints for collectors, and immutable audit events for policy and export changes. Enforce retention and deletion at the storage-segment level, support customer-managed keys only where justified, and expose cost drivers such as bytes ingested, active series, index fields, query scan, and hot-retention days.

implementation_plan.action: Ship a single-region thin slice: authenticated batched ingestion, durable stream, one metric store, one structured-log store, time-bounded query APIs, tenant quotas, and service health telemetry.
Add policy-driven validation, redaction, deduplication, cardinality controls, rollups, dashboards, usage reporting, and replay from raw object storage.
Add durable alert state, idempotent notification connectors, hot-warm-cold retention, query admission control, and noisy-neighbor load tests.
Introduce multi-region replication and failover, residency-aware routing, disaster-recovery exercises, SLO dashboards, and capacity and cost automation.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would first clarify signal scope, ingestion volume, freshness, retention, query patterns, and tenant isolation. My design puts regional OpenTelemetry collectors in front of an authenticated ingestion gateway. The gateway validates, redacts, rate-limits, and durably appends accepted batches to a replicated stream before acknowledging. Separate processors deduplicate retries, compute metric rollups, build log indexes, and archive immutable raw data. Metrics go to a time-series store for low-latency dashboards and alerts; logs go to a columnar indexed store for bounded searches, with object storage for cold retention. A tenant-aware query gateway fans out only to relevant shards and enforces scan budgets. Alerting is a persisted state machine with an outbox for idempotent notifications. I would explicitly cap label cardinality, isolate noisy tenants, expose dropped-data and lag metrics, and choose at-least-once ingestion with deduplication rather than claim end-to-end exactly-once. I would launch single-region, then add tiering and tested regional failover.

level_expectations.mid_level: Clarifies scope and scale, separates ingestion from querying with a durable queue, chooses appropriate metric and log stores, defines basic APIs, and discusses retention, alerting, sharding, backpressure, and access control.
level_expectations.senior: Quantifies SLO and cost drivers, reasons about cardinality and skew, defines acknowledgment and duplicate semantics, designs tenant-aware admission control and alert state, separates hot and cold paths, and explains regional failure, privacy, replay, and migration tradeoffs.

cases.title: Design a system to schedule jobs in a distributed environment.

source_question.title: Design a system to schedule jobs in a distributed environment.

cases.customer_scenario: A global data and AI platform lets enterprise tenants schedule one-time, recurring, and dependency-driven jobs that run customer-provided task types across regional worker pools. Jobs range from seconds to hours, may require CPU, GPU, or tenant-specific network access, and must survive scheduler or worker failures. Customers need predictable start-time SLAs, priorities, cancellation, retries, execution history, and strong tenant isolation without the system pretending arbitrary side effects can be exactly once.
discovery_questions: Which schedule forms are required: one-time timestamps, cron expressions, fixed intervals, dependency graphs, or event-triggered jobs?
How many active schedules, due jobs per second, and peak bursts must the system support in each region?
How strict is start-time accuracy, and how should daylight-saving changes, time zones, clock skew, and missed schedules be handled?
What are the maximum runtime, resource classes, concurrency limits, and placement constraints for jobs?
What delivery semantic is acceptable: at-most-once, at-least-once with idempotency, or fenced singleton execution for selected jobs?
How should retries, backoff, timeout, cancellation, dependency failure, and poison jobs behave?
Do tenants need priorities, fairness, quotas, reservations, or per-job service-level objectives?
What regional failover, data residency, audit, secret access, and customer-code isolation requirements apply?
functional_requirements: Create, update, pause, resume, delete, and inspect one-time or recurring schedules with explicit time-zone and misfire policy.
Materialize each due occurrence as an immutable job run and dispatch it to an eligible regional queue without double-materializing the same occurrence.
Lease jobs to workers, renew heartbeats for long work, detect expired leases, and retry according to a versioned policy.
Support priority, resource class, tenant concurrency limits, placement constraints, cancellation, and dead-letter handling.
Expose job-run state, attempt history, logs, outputs, failure reason, and audit history.
Support dependency-driven workflows by releasing downstream runs only when their predecessor policy is satisfied.
non_functional_requirements: Scale to millions of stored schedules and high burst rates by partitioning schedule ownership and dispatch queues.
Start at least 99% of eligible jobs within 30 seconds of due time under normal load, with priority-specific SLOs.
Durably retain accepted schedules and job-run transitions, with no silent loss of acknowledged work.
Provide 99.95% control-plane availability and continue running already-dispatched jobs during a scheduler control-plane interruption.
Use at-least-once dispatch by default and guarantee one durable JobRun record per schedule occurrence through an idempotent uniqueness key.
Enforce tenant quotas, fair scheduling, workload identity, secret isolation, network policy, and auditable administrative actions.
Recover from a regional scheduler failure within a defined RTO while preventing two regions from concurrently owning the same schedule partition.

core_entities.name: Schedule
core_entities.purpose: Stores tenant, expression, time zone, next fire time, misfire policy, target task, priority, constraints, and version.

core_entities.name: JobDefinition
core_entities.purpose: Describes the executable task type, immutable artifact version, parameters schema, resource request, timeout, and retry policy.

core_entities.name: JobRun
core_entities.purpose: Represents one immutable scheduled occurrence with due time, state, priority, placement, and idempotency key.

core_entities.name: Attempt
core_entities.purpose: Records each leased execution, worker, lease token, heartbeat, timestamps, exit status, and failure reason.

core_entities.name: Worker
core_entities.purpose: Advertises region, resource class, capabilities, health, capacity, and current leases.

core_entities.name: QueueShard
core_entities.purpose: Buffers ready JobRuns partitioned by region, resource class, and priority for competing consumers.

core_entities.name: DependencyEdge
core_entities.purpose: Defines predecessor conditions required before a downstream JobRun becomes ready.

api_interface.purpose: Create a schedule with expression, time zone, task version, constraints, retry policy, and client idempotency key.
Version a mutable schedule change using optimistic concurrency so already-materialized runs remain immutable.
Pause future materialization without terminating running attempts.
Submit an immediate one-time job and return its durable JobRun identifier.
Return current state, attempts, timestamps, output reference, and failure metadata.
Record a durable cancellation request and signal the active worker if one exists.
Renew a worker lease using an opaque fencing token and report progress.
Atomically finish the attempt and transition the JobRun only if the fencing token is current.

component_flow: 1. The control-plane API authenticates the tenant, validates the schedule and task version, enforces quotas, and commits the Schedule to a strongly consistent metadata store with a computed next_fire_at value.
2. Schedule rows are partitioned by a stable schedule ID hash; one active scheduler leader owns each partition through a renewable lease or consensus-backed assignment.

3. Each leader scans an indexed time window for due schedules, then in one transaction inserts a JobRun keyed by schedule_id plus scheduled_time and advances next_fire_at according to the schedule's version and misfire policy.
4. A transactional outbox publishes the committed JobRun to a durable ready queue selected by region, resource class, and priority; an outbox relay retries safely with the JobRun ID as message ID.

5. Eligible workers act as competing consumers. A worker receives a message under a lease, asks the execution service for an Attempt and fencing token, and starts the pinned task artifact in an isolated runtime.
6. The worker heartbeats to renew the lease. Completion writes output metadata and changes Attempt and JobRun state only if the fencing token still owns the run, then acknowledges the queue message.
7. If a worker crashes or its lease expires, a reaper marks the attempt lost and either creates a delayed retry with backoff or dead-letters the run after the retry budget is exhausted.
8. A dependency evaluator consumes terminal JobRun events, updates dependency counters idempotently, and enqueues downstream runs when their policy is satisfied.
9. Status APIs and event streams read materialized execution history, while observability tracks scheduling lag, queue age, lease expiry, retry rate, fairness, and dead-letter depth.
tradeoffs: Polling an indexed due-time table is easy to reason about and recover, but it creates periodic read load; broker-delayed messages reduce polling but make very long schedules, updates, and failover harder to manage.
A single scheduler leader simplifies ordering but caps throughput and increases blast radius; partition leaders scale but require ownership leases, rebalancing, and fencing.

At-least-once delivery prevents silent loss but permits duplicate attempts; at-most-once can lose work, while true exactly-once external side effects are generally impossible without cooperation from the target system.
More priority queues provide isolation and simpler SLOs but increase operational overhead; one shared queue improves utilization but needs fair scheduling and starvation prevention.
Pushing full payloads through the broker simplifies workers but hits message-size and privacy limits; claim-check references add storage reads and lifecycle management.
Active-active multi-region scheduling lowers failover time but makes ownership and duplicate prevention harder; a home-region or active-passive model is simpler with a larger RTO.
failure_security_challenges: A scheduler can crash after creating a JobRun but before publishing it; use a transactional outbox and an idempotent relay rather than a non-atomic database-plus-queue dual write.
Two schedulers can believe they own a partition after a pause or network split; use renewable ownership plus monotonically increasing fencing epochs checked on every materialization write.
A worker can finish after its lease expires and a replacement starts; reject stale completion with a fencing token and require downstream effects to use the JobRun idempotency key where possible.
Queue peek-lock or equivalent delivery can redeliver after worker failure; settle only after durable completion and make all state transitions compare-and-swap and idempotent.
A tenant can flood expensive jobs or monopolize GPU workers; enforce admission quotas, weighted fair queues, per-tenant concurrency, and resource reservations.
Cron schedules around daylight-saving transitions can fire twice or not at all; store the original time zone, define overlap and gap semantics, and persist the resolved UTC occurrence key.
Poison jobs can retry forever; bound attempts and runtime, use exponential backoff with jitter, move exhausted runs to a dead-letter state, and provide controlled replay.

Customer code can exfiltrate secrets or attack neighbors; run immutable artifacts in sandboxed identities with least-privilege secret scopes, network egress policy, signed artifacts, and resource limits.

Regional failover can create duplicate ownership; promote only after a lease or epoch decision in a surviving consistency domain, then reconcile outbox and running-attempt state before broad dispatch.

deep_dives.title: Due-time indexing and partition ownership
deep_dives.details: Index schedules by partition and next_fire_at so each leader scans only a short look-ahead window. Materialization must atomically insert a JobRun with a uniqueness key of tenant, schedule, resolved UTC occurrence, and schedule version while advancing next_fire_at. Partition leases spread work; an epoch on the lease fences delayed leaders after rebalancing. A bounded look-ahead lowers dispatch latency without loading the entire future schedule set into memory.

deep_dives.title: Delivery semantics, leases, and fencing
deep_dives.details: Use at-least-once queue delivery and make JobRun and Attempt transitions idempotent. The queue lock prevents concurrent delivery only temporarily; the execution service therefore issues a monotonically increasing fencing token per attempt. Heartbeat and completion operations compare that token, so a paused worker cannot overwrite a newer attempt. Exactly-once business effects require a downstream idempotency key, conditional write, or transactional integration; the scheduler alone cannot guarantee them.

deep_dives.title: Fairness, priority, and backpressure
deep_dives.details: Partition ready work by resource class and use a small number of priority bands. Within each band, schedule tenants with weighted deficit round robin or virtual finish time, enforcing per-tenant concurrency and global downstream limits. Age low-priority jobs to prevent starvation. Scale workers on oldest-message age and queue depth, but cap aggregate concurrency to avoid moving overload into databases or model endpoints.

deep_dives.title: Misfires, retries, and dependency workflows
deep_dives.details: Every schedule specifies whether a missed interval is skipped, coalesced into one run, or caught up within a maximum count. Retries are new Attempts of the same JobRun, preserving one logical occurrence and stable idempotency key. Dependencies consume terminal events through idempotent counters; a failed predecessor can fail, skip, or still release downstream work according to an explicit policy.

implementation_plan.action: Build a single-region MVP for immediate and one-time jobs with durable JobRun state, transactional outbox, one ready queue, leased workers, heartbeats, cancellation, and idempotent completion.
Add partitioned recurring schedules, time-zone and misfire semantics, leader leases with fencing epochs, retries, dead-letter replay, and schedule-lag observability.
Add resource-class and priority queues, tenant fairness and quotas, autoscaling safeguards, dependency workflows, artifact signing, and sandboxed workload identities.
Add regional replication and controlled promotion, reconcile in-flight work during disaster tests, publish RPO and RTO, and load-test burst scheduling, hot tenants, clock skew, and worker loss.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would clarify schedule types, due-time accuracy, volume, job duration, resource constraints, and delivery semantics. The control plane stores each schedule with its next fire time in a partitioned, strongly consistent metadata store. A leased leader per partition scans a short due-time window and transactionally creates one JobRun per schedule occurrence while advancing the schedule. A transactional outbox then publishes the run to a durable queue, avoiding the database-and-broker dual-write gap. Workers are competing consumers: they lease a message, obtain an attempt fencing token, execute the pinned artifact, heartbeat, and acknowledge only after a token-checked durable completion. Expired leases create a new attempt with backoff, so delivery is at least once and task handlers must be idempotent. I would partition queues by region and resource class, use a few priority bands with tenant fairness, and track oldest-job age, schedule lag, retries, and dead letters. Multi-region promotion must fence the old owner before dispatch resumes.

level_expectations.mid_level: Defines schedule and run state, uses durable queues and stateless workers, explains leases, retries, cancellation, sharding, priorities, and basic monitoring, and recognizes duplicate execution risk.
level_expectations.senior: Closes the metadata-to-queue dual-write gap, defines occurrence and attempt idempotency, uses partition epochs and fencing tokens, handles misfires and time zones, protects downstream systems with fairness and backpressure, and gives credible multi-region failover semantics without claiming impossible exactly-once side effects.

cases.title: Design a Secure, Scalable User Login System
cases.customer_scenario: A global payments platform needs a first-party login service for customer-facing web and mobile applications. It must authenticate consumers and business users, support password and passwordless factors, protect high-risk accounts, and issue revocable sessions without making every application implement credential security independently. This is an interview adaptation, not a claim about Stripe's or Visa's production architecture.
discovery_questions: Who signs in: consumers, merchant employees, administrators, partners, or all of them, and must one person belong to several organizations?
Which clients must be supported: server-rendered web, single-page applications, native mobile apps, command-line tools, or public APIs?
What are the peak login and token-refresh rates, regional traffic distribution, availability SLO, and acceptable interactive-login latency?
Which authentication methods are required at launch: password, passkey, email link, social or enterprise federation, and recovery codes?
When must the system require step-up authentication, and which signals may the risk engine use without violating privacy rules?
What session lifetime, idle timeout, remember-me policy, device limit, and global sign-out behavior does the business require?
Which regulatory, data-residency, audit-retention, and account-deletion obligations apply to identity and security telemetry?
During an identity-provider or regional outage, should existing sessions continue while new logins fail closed?
functional_requirements: Register a user, verify ownership of an email or phone identifier, and enforce uniqueness according to the product's account-linking policy.
Authenticate with a password or supported passwordless authenticator and add MFA or step-up verification when policy requires it.
Issue short-lived access credentials plus a longer-lived, rotatable session or refresh credential after successful authentication.
Refresh, inspect, list, and revoke sessions by device; support current-device logout and logout from all devices.
Recover an account through expiring, single-use challenges without revealing whether an identifier exists.
Record security-relevant events and notify the user about new devices, credential changes, recovery, and suspicious activity.
non_functional_requirements: Target at least 99.99% availability for validation and refresh paths; interactive login may degrade independently from established-session validation.
Keep cached access-token validation local to the application or gateway and target a p99 under 100 ms for online session checks within a region.
Scale horizontally through bursty login events while rate limiting by account, device, IP reputation, network, and global abuse signals.
Protect credentials and tokens in transit and at rest, never log secrets, use phishing-resistant factors where available, and follow least privilege.
Provide strongly consistent credential changes, challenge consumption, refresh-token rotation, and revocation writes, while allowing eventually consistent analytics.
Maintain immutable, privacy-filtered audit records with traceable request IDs and configurable retention and regional placement.
Support key rotation without downtime by publishing overlapping verification keys and retaining old keys through the maximum token-validation window.

core_entities.name: User
core_entities.purpose: Stable person identity with status, verified identifiers, security policy references, and organization memberships.

core_entities.name: Credential
core_entities.purpose: Password verifier or external credential binding; stores algorithm metadata and rotation state, never a recoverable plaintext password.

core_entities.name: Authenticator

core_entities.name: LoginAttempt
core_entities.purpose: Short-lived state for an authentication transaction, including risk result, required factors, failure count, and correlation ID.

core_entities.name: VerificationChallenge
core_entities.purpose: Hashed, expiring, purpose-bound, single-use proof for email verification, password reset, or step-up authentication.

core_entities.name: Session
core_entities.purpose: Server-controlled login state bound to a user and device, with created, last-used, expiry, assurance, and revocation attributes.

core_entities.name: RefreshTokenFamily
core_entities.purpose: Tracks rotated refresh credentials and detects reuse of an already-consumed token so the entire family can be revoked.

api_interface.purpose: Create a pending user and send an out-of-band identifier-verification challenge; accept an idempotency key.
Consume a single-use verification challenge and activate or update the verified identifier.
Submit an identifier and primary proof, returning either a session or a transaction requiring another factor.
Complete the required MFA or passkey step for one bounded login attempt.
Rotate a valid refresh credential and issue a new short-lived access token and refresh credential.
Revoke the current session, clear the browser cookie, and make the operation idempotent.
List active devices and sessions without returning token material.
Revoke one session; a reserved all-sessions operation supports global sign-out.
Start account recovery with a uniform response and abuse controls that prevent account enumeration.

component_flow: The client sends a login request through an edge gateway that terminates TLS, applies coarse bot and volumetric controls, and assigns a correlation ID.
The authentication API normalizes the identifier, retrieves the user and credential metadata, and performs a constant-shape response whether or not the user exists.
A credential worker verifies the password with a memory-hard hash or validates the passkey assertion; sensitive work is isolated and concurrency-limited.
The risk and policy service evaluates recent failures, device reputation, location change, account role, and requested action, then decides allow, deny, or require step-up.
If another factor is required, the challenge service creates a hashed, expiring, purpose-bound challenge and delivers it through an isolated notification provider.
After all required proofs succeed, the session service atomically creates a server session and refresh-token family and emits a security event through an outbox.
The token service signs a short-lived access token with the active key; the web client receives an opaque Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookie or a platform-secured mobile credential.
Applications validate signed access tokens from cached metadata for routine requests and perform an online session or revocation check for sensitive operations.
Refresh rotates the refresh credential in a single transaction; reuse of a consumed token revokes its family and creates an alert.
Logout or credential reset updates revocation state first, clears the client cookie, and asynchronously delivers notifications and analytics events.
tradeoffs: Stateless signed access tokens reduce central read load and survive brief auth-service outages, but revocation is delayed until expiry unless sensitive paths also check session state.
Opaque server sessions provide immediate revocation and smaller browser credentials, but every cache miss adds a network dependency and creates a hot session store.
A shared authentication service centralizes policy and security expertise, but its blast radius is larger than independently implemented application login.
Aggressive adaptive MFA reduces account takeover, but false positives create support load and can lock legitimate users out during travel or device replacement.
Multi-region active-active reads improve latency and availability, while globally ordered credential and refresh-token mutations are more expensive and may need a home-region or quorum design.
Passkeys resist phishing and credential stuffing, but recovery, legacy-client support, and authenticator synchronization still require carefully designed fallback paths.
failure_security_challenges: Credential stuffing and password spraying target many accounts with leaked credentials; defend with breached-password checks, layered rate limits, risk scoring, and MFA rather than IP blocking alone.
Account enumeration leaks through status codes, response text, timing, recovery delivery, or rate-limit behavior; keep externally visible behavior uniform and monitor internally.
A stolen refresh token is replayed after legitimate rotation; use sender constraints where practical, store only token hashes, rotate every use, and revoke the family on reuse.
Concurrent refresh requests race and one looks like theft; define a narrow grace or compare-and-swap policy that tolerates benign retries without allowing indefinite replay.
Signing-key compromise lets an attacker mint tokens; keep private keys in an HSM-backed service, restrict signing access, rotate, publish key IDs, and maintain emergency revocation procedures.
Notification-provider compromise exposes reset links or enables phishing; use single-use short TTL challenges, provider isolation, redacted messages, and an in-product recovery confirmation.
A primary identity region fails after credentials are verified but before a session commit; make transaction boundaries explicit and retry with an idempotent login-attempt identifier.
Logs or traces accidentally capture passwords, one-time codes, cookies, or tokens; enforce structured allowlisted telemetry and automated secret scanning.

deep_dives.title: Credential verification and account recovery
deep_dives.details: Store a unique salt and a memory-hard password verifier with algorithm and cost metadata so parameters can be upgraded after a successful login. Run verification in a bounded worker pool to prevent the hash cost from becoming a denial-of-service amplifier. Recovery challenges are random, hashed at rest, tied to one purpose and account, short-lived, and consumed with a conditional write. Recovery should revoke old sessions, notify existing channels, and avoid weaker knowledge-based questions. Passkeys can become the preferred primary proof, while the fallback path receives equal threat modeling because attackers choose the weakest path.

deep_dives.title: Session, access-token, and refresh-token lifecycle
deep_dives.details: Use short-lived access tokens for low-latency authorization and a server-side session plus refresh-token family for control. A refresh transaction compares the presented token hash, marks it consumed, creates its successor, and commits both changes atomically. Reuse outside the concurrency policy revokes the family. Access-token validators cache issuer metadata and public keys, verify signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and required authorization claims, and refresh unknown keys safely. High-risk actions also check current session assurance and revocation so a recently disabled account cannot rely on token expiry alone.

deep_dives.title: Abuse prevention and adaptive authentication
deep_dives.details: Rate limiting must combine account, IP, network, device, and global signals because any single key is bypassable or harms shared networks. The risk service returns a policy decision rather than exposing raw vendor scores to clients. Low risk proceeds, medium risk requires a stronger enrolled factor, and high risk is blocked or routed to assisted recovery. Security events feed delayed analytics and near-real-time detection, but login correctness must not depend on the analytics pipeline. Keep manual review and false-positive measurement in the rollout plan.

deep_dives.title: Availability and consistency boundaries
deep_dives.details: Token verification should continue from cached keys during a short control-plane outage, and existing sessions can remain usable according to policy. Credential changes, challenge consumption, session creation, refresh rotation, and revocation require consistent writes. Replicate read models and public keys broadly, but choose an explicit home region or consensus-backed store for contested mutations. Fail closed for new proofs when correctness cannot be established; do not silently mint a session from stale credential or revocation state.

implementation_plan.action: Define identity types, assurance levels, session semantics, recovery policy, abuse model, SLOs, regional boundaries, and a threat model before selecting token formats.
Build the minimum password or passkey login, verified identifier, server session, refresh rotation, logout, audit outbox, and local token-validation path behind one pilot application.
Add MFA and step-up policy, device and session management, recovery, layered rate limits, key rotation, security notifications, and operator tooling.

Load-test hash isolation and refresh bursts; red-team enumeration, stuffing, replay, CSRF, XSS token theft, and recovery; then run regional, key-rotation, notification, and datastore failure exercises before progressive rollout.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would separate credential proof, risk policy, session control, and token validation. The edge absorbs bots and assigns a correlation ID; the auth service verifies a memory-hard password hash or passkey and asks the policy service whether step-up is required. On success, the session service atomically creates a revocable session and refresh-token family, while the token service issues a short-lived signed access token. Applications validate those tokens locally from cached keys, but sensitive actions also check live session state. Every refresh rotates the credential, and reuse revokes the family. Recovery uses short-lived, hashed, single-use challenges and never reveals whether an account exists. I would prioritize credential stuffing, refresh replay, recovery abuse, key compromise, and regional failure tests, and I would let established sessions degrade more gracefully than new authentication.

level_expectations.mid_level: Clarifies users and clients, separates authentication from authorization, proposes secure password storage, MFA, sessions, refresh and logout APIs, identifies rate limiting and token theft, and can trace a complete happy-path login.
level_expectations.senior: Defines assurance and consistency boundaries, makes token-versus-session revocation tradeoffs explicit, handles refresh races and key rollover, designs recovery and enumeration defenses, isolates expensive hashing, specifies outage behavior and observability, and drives a staged security validation plan.

cases.title: Multi-Tenant Foundation-Model Sampling API
cases.category: Generative AI Platform and API Design

source_question.title: Design an API that lets a customer sample from large generative models.

cases.customer_scenario: [Adapted scenario] A foundation-model provider wants to offer approved enterprise customers one stable API for one-shot and conversational text generation across several large models. Customers need streaming, bounded sampling controls, predictable quotas, usage reporting, safety enforcement, model-version stability, and strict tenant isolation without receiving direct access to provider credentials or deployment topology.
discovery_questions: What does sample access mean here: a limited beta, a token budget, a restricted model catalog, or probabilistic generation controls?
Which modalities and interaction patterns are in scope for the first release: text, images, audio, tool calls, one-shot requests, or multi-turn chat?
Which sampling controls may customers set, such as temperature, top_p, maximum output tokens, stop sequences, number of candidates, and seed?
What are the per-tenant throughput, concurrency, first-token latency, completion-latency, availability, and monthly-budget targets?
Must requests remain in a particular geography, private network, or dedicated deployment for contractual or regulatory reasons?
What authentication model is required for server workloads and human developers, and how quickly must access be revocable?
May prompts, outputs, safety decisions, and token counts be retained; if so, for how long and under which redaction and customer-controlled logging policies?
How should model upgrades work: automatic aliases, pinned versions, deprecation windows, compatibility tests, or customer opt-in?
What safety policy applies to inputs and outputs, and which blocked or truncated outcomes must be distinguishable to clients?
Should long-running generations be synchronous only, or do customers need asynchronous status, cancellation, callbacks, and batch jobs?
functional_requirements: List the model aliases, supported capabilities, context limits, lifecycle status, and allowed sampling parameters available to the authenticated tenant.
Accept a one-shot or multi-turn generation request containing customer input, optional context, model alias, sampling parameters, safety metadata, and a client idempotency key.
Return either a normal JSON result or a server-sent event stream containing ordered deltas, a terminal reason, token usage, safety status, request ID, and resolved model version.
Create and continue optional chat sessions while enforcing a bounded context policy and allowing customers to delete retained session state.
Enforce per-tenant model entitlements, token and request quotas, concurrency limits, maximum input/output size, and budget policy before model invocation.
Route an accepted request to a healthy compatible deployment and apply bounded failover without exposing backend credentials or region topology.
Expose request status and cancellation for asynchronous or disconnected clients and make cancellation best effort once generation has started.
Provide tenant-scoped usage and audit records for chargeback, troubleshooting, safety review, and quota planning without exposing another tenant's data.
non_functional_requirements: [Proposed target] Achieve 99.9% monthly availability for the gateway while publishing model-specific availability separately.
[Proposed target] Add no more than 100 ms p95 gateway overhead before backend inference, excluding content-safety and model time.
Scale horizontally while preserving per-tenant fairness so a noisy customer cannot consume the shared token or concurrency pool.
Provide tenant isolation in authorization, caches, session storage, logs, metrics, and quota counters; never use prompt text as a cache key visible across tenants.
Encrypt traffic in transit and data at rest, use short-lived identity-based backend authentication, and support private connectivity and regional routing where required.
Make request acceptance, usage accounting, and audit events durable and traceable by request ID while treating retries as at-least-once delivery.
Keep prompt and completion bodies out of operational logs by default and support configurable retention, redaction, deletion, and zero-retention modes.
Pin model versions behind stable aliases and require compatibility, safety, latency, and quality evaluation before shifting production traffic.
Degrade explicitly under overload with 429 or 503 responses, Retry-After guidance, and no silent model downgrade that changes quality or policy.

core_entities.name: UsageRecord

api_interface.purpose: Return only model aliases and capabilities entitled to the authenticated tenant.
Submit a one-shot or multi-turn generation; honor Idempotency-Key and either return JSON or stream SSE deltas.
Read tenant-scoped status, terminal metadata, usage, and an output reference for asynchronous requests.
Request best-effort cancellation and prevent queued work from starting.
Create an optional conversation container with explicit retention and model-alias policy.
Append a turn and generate the next response using a bounded, server-assembled context.
Delete retained session content subject to the customer contract and audit policy.
Return tenant-scoped token, request, error, and cost-attribution aggregates.

component_flow: A client resolves an allowed model through GET /v1/models and submits POST /v1/responses with an access token, tenant context, and idempotency key.
The edge and API gateway terminate TLS, apply WAF and payload-size rules, validate the token, derive the tenant from trusted claims, and attach a request ID.
The policy layer validates the schema, model entitlement, sampling bounds, regional policy, and input safety; it rejects invalid or disallowed requests before inference.
The quota service performs an atomic admission check for estimated prompt tokens, request rate, concurrency, and remaining budget, then reserves capacity for the request.
The request service writes the canonical request state and idempotency mapping before placing accepted asynchronous work on a durable queue or continuing synchronously.
The router resolves the model alias to a pinned version and chooses a healthy compatible deployment by region, priority, capacity, and circuit-breaker state.
A model adapter converts the canonical request to the provider protocol and authenticates to the backend with managed identity rather than a customer-visible key.
For streaming, the gateway relays ordered deltas with backpressure; after the first byte it does not transparently replay the request to another model because that could duplicate or diverge output.
The output policy checks generated content and emits a clear stop, length, cancellation, or content-filter finish reason rather than presenting a partial response as complete.
The metering path reconciles estimated and actual tokens, releases concurrency, writes an immutable usage record, and updates redacted latency, safety, saturation, and error metrics.

If the selected backend returns 429 or a retriable failure before output begins, the router respects Retry-After, opens the circuit when appropriate, and makes a bounded attempt on a compatible deployment.
The client receives the terminal event and can query status by response ID; duplicate submissions with the same tenant and idempotency key return the original operation rather than starting new work.
tradeoffs: A provider-neutral canonical API reduces client coupling, but it can hide unique model features; expose a strict common core plus versioned capability extensions rather than arbitrary pass-through fields.
Synchronous streaming gives the best interactive experience, while asynchronous jobs survive disconnects and simplify retries; supporting both increases state-machine and billing complexity.
Shared deployments maximize utilization and model choice, while dedicated or provisioned capacity improves isolation and predictable latency at higher idle cost.

Priority-based failover improves availability, but cross-region routing can violate residency constraints and a different model version can change behavior; fail over only within an explicitly compatible policy set.
Server-managed sessions simplify clients, while stateless requests improve privacy and portability; make sessions optional with explicit retention and context-truncation rules.
Pre-admission token estimation prevents obvious quota overruns, but exact usage is known only after generation; reserve pessimistically, reconcile actual usage, and tolerate bounded counter drift.

Semantic caching can reduce cost and latency, but generative outputs depend on policy, model version, sampling settings, and tenant data; default to no cross-tenant cache and use only for deterministic, approved workloads.
failure_security_challenges: A tenant tampers with a tenant ID, model name, or quota key; derive identity and authorization from validated claims and server-owned entitlement data, never from untrusted body fields.
One customer exhausts token, request, or connection capacity; use tenant-scoped admission control, weighted fairness, concurrency bulkheads, and hard output-token limits.
Backend throttling or regional failure causes retry storms; honor Retry-After, use jittered client guidance, priority pools, bounded retries, and circuit breakers.
A stream disconnects after partial output; persist terminal state and usage, allow status lookup, and do not replay automatically after bytes have been delivered.
An idempotent retry arrives while the first request is still running; atomically bind tenant plus idempotency key to one operation and return the same operation state.
A prompt or completion violates safety policy; reject unsafe inputs, stop or annotate unsafe outputs, return a machine-readable finish reason, and avoid logging the sensitive body by default.
A model alias changes behavior unexpectedly; pin versions, canary traffic, run regression and safety evaluations, and provide deprecation windows and rollback.

Usage accounting differs from backend billing because a timeout or filtered response still consumed tokens; write attempt-level records and reconcile gateway estimates against backend usage asynchronously.
Logs, traces, or caches leak prompts across tenants; redact bodies, partition every store and key by tenant, encrypt sensitive fields, restrict operator access, and test for cross-tenant access.
Cancellation races with completion; model cancellation as a monotonic state transition and make downstream metering idempotent even if the backend finishes after the client cancels.

deep_dives.title: Stable API contract, streaming, and idempotency
deep_dives.details: Use a canonical request envelope with an explicit model alias, input messages, bounded sampling controls, stream flag, metadata limits, and optional session ID. Return a request ID, resolved model version, output items, usage, and a typed finish reason. SSE events carry sequence numbers and end with one terminal event. Idempotency is scoped to tenant plus endpoint plus key and stores a hash of the normalized request; reuse with a different body returns 409. Before any output, a retriable attempt may move to another compatible deployment. After output begins, automatic replay is unsafe because stochastic generations diverge, so the stream ends with a retriable error and the client chooses whether to start a new response.

deep_dives.title: Capacity routing, fairness, and overload behavior
deep_dives.details: Admission control occurs before expensive inference. Maintain approximate fast counters for requests and estimated tokens, a concurrency lease per tenant and model, and durable usage for reconciliation. The router filters by entitlement, version, modality, and residency, then ranks healthy deployments by priority and available capacity. A circuit breaker removes backends returning 429 or 5xx until Retry-After expires. Keep tenant bulkheads so premium or dedicated capacity is not consumed by the shared pool. Return 429 when the caller's quota is exhausted and 503 when provider capacity is unavailable; both include request IDs and retry guidance.

deep_dives.title: Safety, privacy, and tenant isolation
deep_dives.details: Apply schema, size, malware, and prompt-safety checks before model invocation and completion checks before delivery. Treat filter configuration as a versioned policy referenced in the audit record. Use managed identity between the gateway and model deployments, private endpoints where required, least-privilege roles, and customer-controlled retention. Operational telemetry contains hashes, counts, policy labels, model versions, and latency rather than prompt text. Sessions, idempotency records, quotas, caches, and object storage are all partitioned and authorized by server-derived tenant identity.

deep_dives.title: Model lifecycle and evaluation
deep_dives.details: A customer-facing alias resolves to a pinned model and policy version. Build an evaluation suite from allowed customer workflows and adversarial prompts, measuring task quality, refusal behavior, safety, latency, first-token time, token use, and contract compatibility. Shift a small tenant-safe cohort to the candidate version, compare results, and roll back automatically on guardrail regressions. Publish deprecation dates and never silently switch to a cheaper or weaker model when a request names a pinned alias.

implementation_plan.action: Define the beta scope, canonical request and response schema, model-alias contract, tenant entitlements, retention policy, safety policy, SLOs, quotas, error taxonomy, and evaluation set.

Deliver a single-region thin slice with Entra-based client authentication, API Management, one pinned model deployment, managed-identity backend access, streaming, idempotency, token metering, and redacted telemetry.

Add atomic admission control, per-tenant fairness, asynchronous status and cancellation, session retention controls, multiple compatible deployments, health-aware routing, circuit breakers, and usage reconciliation.
Run load, quota, disconnect, failover, privacy, abuse, model-regression, and billing-reconciliation tests; canary selected tenants, publish dashboards and runbooks, then expand models and regions.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would first clarify whether sample means beta access, usage limits, or sampling controls, then expose a stable multi-tenant responses API with optional SSE streaming and sessions. The gateway authenticates the caller, derives tenant identity from claims, validates model entitlement and sampling bounds, runs safety checks, and atomically reserves request, token, concurrency, and budget quota. A router maps a stable alias to a pinned compatible model version and a healthy regional deployment. Managed identity keeps provider credentials out of clients. Before any bytes are streamed, 429 or 5xx failures can fail over through a circuit breaker; after streaming begins, I would not replay a stochastic request. Every response includes request ID, finish reason, resolved version, and usage. I would partition state and telemetry by tenant, avoid prompt logging by default, reconcile usage asynchronously, and gate model upgrades with quality, safety, latency, and compatibility evaluations.

level_expectations.mid_level: Clarifies the meaning of sampling, defines a usable request and streaming response, identifies authentication, quotas, model routing, safety, tenant isolation, storage, and basic retries, and can trace one request end to end.
level_expectations.senior: Makes ambiguity and customer constraints drive the design; distinguishes admission, routing, execution, streaming, and metering; handles idempotency and partial-stream semantics; designs tenant fairness, circuit breaking, privacy, model lifecycle, evaluation, and cost controls; and explains a staged rollout with measurable SLOs and failure tests.

cases.title: Secure Enterprise RAG over Private Customer Data

source_question.title: Design a retrieval-augmented generation system over a customer's private data.

cases.customer_scenario: [Adapted scenario] A multinational engineering company wants an internal assistant over private SharePoint, Azure Data Lake, support-ticket, and policy content. Employees must receive concise answers with page-level citations, only from documents they are already authorized to read. The system must ingest updates incrementally, support legal deletion and regional boundaries, resist prompt injection in uploaded documents, and decline when retrieval evidence is insufficient.
discovery_questions: Which repositories, file types, languages, media, document structures, and total corpus size are in scope?
How often does each source change, and what freshness or deletion SLA is required from source update to searchable index?
What is the authoritative access model: user, group, document ACL, folder inheritance, tenant, region, classification, or a combination?
Must the system mirror source-system permissions at query time, and how quickly must permission revocations take effect?
Which user journeys and question types matter most, and what representative questions, source passages, expected answers, and no-answer cases exist?
What quality thresholds define success for retrieval recall, citation correctness, groundedness, completeness, refusal, and user usefulness?
What latency, concurrency, availability, token-cost, ingestion-cost, and peak-load targets apply?
Can private data leave a region or network boundary, and may prompts, retrieved chunks, answers, and feedback be retained for debugging or evaluation?
Should the assistant only answer questions, or may it call tools or modify source systems, and which actions require approval?
How should conflicting, superseded, duplicate, or low-trust documents be ranked and disclosed to the user?
Which adversaries are in scope: malicious users, compromised source content, prompt injection, poisoned indexes, operator misuse, or cross-tenant access?
functional_requirements: Register approved private data sources and perform initial plus incremental ingestion while preserving source URI, version, timestamps, classification, and access-control metadata.
Parse, normalize, deduplicate, structurally chunk, enrich, embed, and index supported content with stable document and chunk identities.
Authenticate every user and apply source-derived document authorization before or during retrieval so unauthorized chunks never enter the prompt.
Run hybrid lexical and vector retrieval with metadata filters and optional semantic reranking, then package only the best authorized evidence within a token budget.
Generate an answer constrained to retrieved evidence, attach verifiable document and page or section citations, and decline or ask a clarifying question when evidence is weak.
Expose source and ingestion status, including failed documents, stale permissions, deletion progress, and last successful checkpoint.
Propagate document updates, permission changes, and deletions idempotently without rebuilding the entire corpus.
Capture explicit user feedback and evaluation traces linked to retrieval and prompt versions while respecting private-data logging policy.
non_functional_requirements: No cross-user, cross-group, cross-tenant, or cross-region data leakage; authorization is deterministic and independent of model judgment.
[Proposed target] Return the first answer token within 3 seconds at p95 for normal interactive queries and complete the answer within 8 seconds at p95, subject to model choice.
[Proposed target] Make source content, ACL changes, and deletions searchable or absent within 15 minutes at p95 for incremental connectors.
[Proposed target] Achieve 99.9% monthly availability for the query API and expose degraded retrieval or model states explicitly.
Encrypt data in transit and at rest, use managed identities and private endpoints, and restrict outbound traffic and operator privileges.
Keep raw prompts, chunks, and answers out of default logs; provide configurable retention, redaction, deletion, and audit controls.
Scale ingestion independently from online query traffic and prevent a large source crawl or tenant from starving interactive requests.
Version parsers, chunking, embeddings, index schema, retrieval parameters, prompts, model, and safety policy so an answer can be reproduced and regressions rolled back.
Continuously measure retrieval and answer quality on representative, adversarial, permission, and no-answer test sets rather than relying only on model fluency.
Control cost with incremental processing, bounded top-k and context size, model routing, duplicate suppression, and per-tenant budgets.

core_entities.purpose: Captures the authenticated question, conversation context reference, filters, and retrieval policy version.

core_entities.name: RetrievalTrace
core_entities.purpose: Records redacted query transformations, authorized result IDs, scores, reranking, latency, and version metadata for evaluation.

core_entities.name: Answer

api_interface.purpose: Register an approved source by reference to server-side connection configuration; never accept reusable source secrets in normal request bodies.
Start or request an idempotent incremental synchronization from the last durable checkpoint.
Return checkpoint, progress, failed-document reasons, freshness, and index publication status.
Request tombstoning and deletion of all chunks, vectors, cached context, and retained content for an authorized document.
Retrieve authorized evidence and return or stream a grounded answer with citations, refusal reason, and request ID.
Return the caller-authorized cited passages and lineage used for an answer, subject to current access checks.
Record a rating and issue category without allowing the client to overwrite the original trace.
Run a versioned offline evaluation over approved examples before publishing an index, retrieval, prompt, or model change.

component_flow: A connector uses managed identity or a vault-referenced credential to read only an approved source partition, including content, version, deletion markers, and authoritative ACL metadata.
The ingestion coordinator resumes from a durable checkpoint, assigns stable document IDs, emits idempotent work items, and isolates poison documents in a dead-letter path.
Parsers extract text, layout, tables, page boundaries, and source lineage in a sandbox; malware, unsupported content, and embedded instruction patterns are flagged for policy handling.

The pipeline normalizes and deduplicates content, creates structure-aware chunks with overlap where justified, and attaches document version, page, classification, trust, region, and ACL fields to every chunk.
An embedding worker generates vectors with a pinned embedding model, while the index writer upserts text, vector, metadata, and authorization fields into a versioned Azure AI Search index.
Only after document chunks and permission metadata are complete does the publisher advance the source checkpoint; deletions create tombstones and remove all derived artifacts idempotently.
At query time, Microsoft Entra authenticates the employee; the API derives tenant, user, and group claims from the validated identity and resolves current authorization policy.
A query planner normalizes the question, adds conversation context within a budget, generates lexical and vector queries, and constructs server-side region, classification, and ACL filters.

Azure AI Search executes hybrid retrieval over only authorized content; semantic reranking or an application reranker orders the best passages, and a score or evidence threshold can trigger a no-answer path.
The orchestrator deduplicates passages, favors authoritative and current versions, packs evidence within the context budget, labels each passage as untrusted data, and gives it an opaque citation ID.
The model receives system instructions, the user question, and authorized evidence; it must answer from that evidence, cite citation IDs, report conflicts, and decline when support is missing.
A postprocessor validates that citations resolve to retrieved chunks, strips unsupported links or leaked system text, applies output safety policy, and streams the answer and citation metadata.
The service writes redacted operational metrics and a versioned retrieval trace, while raw prompt and chunk retention follows the tenant's explicit policy.

User feedback and offline evaluation compare retrieval recall, citation correctness, groundedness, no-answer behavior, permission enforcement, latency, and cost before a candidate index or prompt becomes active.
tradeoffs: Larger chunks preserve context and reduce index rows, while smaller chunks improve retrieval precision and context packing; select by document structure and measured retrieval performance rather than one global size.

Vector search handles semantic paraphrases, while lexical search handles exact identifiers, dates, names, and codes; hybrid retrieval improves coverage but requires score fusion, reranking, and more evaluation.
Pre-filtering by ACL minimizes leakage and wasted retrieval, while post-filtering is easier to bolt on but risks side channels and too few results; authorization should constrain the search itself.

Copying ACLs into the index enables fast query-time filtering, while live source authorization is fresher but adds latency and dependency risk; mirror ACLs with event-driven refresh and define a revocation SLA.
A managed indexer reduces custom ingestion code, while a custom pipeline gives better parser, ACL, chunking, quarantine, and version control at higher operational cost.
One shared tenant-partitioned index is efficient, while per-tenant or per-region indexes provide stronger isolation and easier deletion at higher cost and management overhead.

Server-managed conversation history improves follow-up questions, while stateless requests simplify privacy and reproducibility; store only when needed and re-authorize retrieved evidence on every turn.
More retrieved passages can improve recall, but increase latency, token cost, distraction, and injection surface; rerank and enforce a small evidence budget.
Re-embedding in place is simple but mixes incompatible vectors during rollout; dual indexes support safe comparison and rollback but temporarily double storage and ingestion cost.
failure_security_challenges: A document's ACL is missing, stale, or mapped to the wrong identity, causing unauthorized retrieval; default deny, validate ACL completeness, test revocation, and fail publication when security metadata is absent.

A malicious document contains indirect prompt instructions; treat retrieved text as untrusted data, detect and quarantine suspicious content, separate instructions from evidence, and prohibit the model from authorizing actions.
A connector checkpoint advances before all chunks are durable; commit publication only after successful idempotent writes and retain replayable source versions or event IDs.
Parser, OCR, embedding, or indexing failures leave partial documents; use per-document state, bounded retries, dead-letter queues, visible freshness, and atomic version publication.
A deleted or revoked document remains in vectors, caches, conversation memory, evaluation data, or logs; maintain lineage and tombstones that fan out deletion to every derived store.
Poor chunking or retrieval returns plausible but irrelevant evidence; use representative labeled queries, retrieval metrics, hybrid search, reranking, thresholds, and an explicit no-answer behavior.
The model invents citations or claims not present in evidence; use opaque citation IDs, validate them against the retrieval set, measure citation entailment, and block unsupported links.

A user infers sensitive content from result counts, snippets, timing, or errors; apply authorization inside retrieval, normalize errors, minimize unauthorized side channels, and audit probing patterns.
An embedding or model upgrade silently degrades quality; pin versions, build a candidate index, run offline and canary evaluations, and switch through an atomic alias with rollback.

Search or model capacity is exhausted; isolate ingestion from online resources, use quotas and backpressure, cache only safe tenant-scoped artifacts, and return a clear degraded or retryable response.
Conflicting or superseded documents produce an unsafe answer; index effective dates and authority metadata, rank current authoritative sources, and make the answer disclose unresolved conflict.
Sensitive prompt or chunk content appears in telemetry or support tooling; log metadata by default, use short retention and redaction, restrict break-glass access, and audit every content view.

deep_dives.title: Incremental ingestion, chunking, and index versioning
deep_dives.details: Give each source object a stable document ID and version and each derived chunk a deterministic ID from tenant, document, version, chunker version, and ordinal. Persist the connector checkpoint only after parsing, ACL capture, chunking, embedding, and index upsert succeed. Choose structure-aware chunks for headings, tables, and pages; retain page lineage and modest overlap only when evaluation shows benefit. Content hashes suppress duplicate work. Build incompatible schema or embedding changes into a candidate index, run evaluation, then atomically move a read alias so rollback does not require reingestion. Tombstones remove chunks and all derived caches by lineage.

deep_dives.title: Authorization and private-data isolation
deep_dives.details: Authentication proves the caller; authorization decides which chunks may be retrieved. Derive tenant, user object ID, groups, region, and classification clearance from trusted identity and policy services. Attach source ACL metadata to every indexed chunk and include a server-constructed filter in lexical and vector retrieval. Missing ACL data is deny-by-default. Never ask the model to filter secrets after retrieval. Recheck current authorization when a user opens cited evidence, because access may have changed since the answer. Use managed identities, private endpoints, least-privilege connector roles, tenant or regional index boundaries where justified, and tests that attempt cross-group and cross-tenant retrieval.

deep_dives.title: Retrieval quality and evidence packing
deep_dives.details: Create a gold set containing questions, relevant passages, expected answers, permission contexts, and intentionally unanswerable cases. Run lexical and vector retrieval in parallel, fuse results, apply metadata filters, rerank, deduplicate adjacent chunks, and prefer current authoritative sources. Measure recall@k, precision@k, mean reciprocal rank or NDCG where useful, plus latency and context-token cost. Tune chunking, embedding, top-k, fusion, and reranking together. If no passage crosses the evidence threshold, ask a clarifying question or decline rather than letting a fluent model improvise.

deep_dives.title: Grounded generation, citations, and evaluation
deep_dives.details: Assign each retrieved passage an opaque citation ID and send it as untrusted evidence beneath a strict system instruction. Require claims to cite those IDs, surface document title and page from stored lineage, and validate every citation against the retrieval set before returning it. Evaluate groundedness, citation correctness, answer completeness, refusal quality, harmful content, latency, and cost. Add adversarial documents and permission-negative examples. Human review remains important for high-impact domains, and low-confidence answers should link users to the source rather than conceal uncertainty.

implementation_plan.action: Define the first user journey, source and authorization model, residency and retention rules, freshness and deletion SLAs, representative corpus, gold questions, expected passages, and no-answer and permission-negative examples.

Build a secure thin slice for one source: managed-identity connector, parser, structure-aware chunker, pinned embeddings, versioned Azure AI Search index, Entra login, ACL-constrained hybrid retrieval, citations, refusal, and redacted telemetry.

Add incremental checkpoints, idempotent update and deletion, dead-letter handling, dual-index rollout, semantic reranking, tenant and regional isolation, private endpoints, prompt-injection defenses, feedback, and evaluation automation.

Test retrieval and groundedness, citation validity, ACL revocation and leakage, poisoned documents, deletion propagation, stale sources, scale, failover, latency, and cost; canary users, publish freshness and quality dashboards, then expand sources.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would separate an asynchronous ingestion plane from the online answer path. Connectors read approved private sources with managed identity, preserve document versions and ACLs, parse and structurally chunk content, add page lineage, create embeddings, and upsert a versioned Azure AI Search index. At query time Entra authenticates the employee, and the application derives tenant, user, group, region, and classification filters from trusted claims. Hybrid lexical and vector search runs only over authorized chunks, then reranking and an evidence threshold choose a small context. The model treats that context as untrusted data, answers only from it, and cites opaque IDs that the API validates back to document pages. Missing evidence produces a decline, not a guess. I would use private endpoints, redacted telemetry, idempotent deletion, and dual-index rollout, then evaluate recall, groundedness, citation correctness, permission leakage, latency, and cost on representative and adversarial test sets.

level_expectations.mid_level: Separates ingestion from querying, proposes chunking, embeddings, a vector or hybrid index, an orchestrator and model, citations, authentication, metadata filters, incremental updates, and basic quality and failure handling.
level_expectations.senior: Starts from corpus, ACL, residency, freshness, and evaluation constraints; enforces authorization inside retrieval; versions every pipeline stage; designs idempotent update and deletion, safe index migration, no-answer behavior, citation validation, injection defenses, privacy-safe observability, and measurable retrieval and answer-quality gates with staged rollout.
