cases.title: Correct Payment Processing Under Failure

source_question.title: Design a payment processing system, accounting for retries, idempotency, and correctness under failure.

cases.customer_scenario: An online marketplace needs a payment service that accepts customer payment attempts, calls one of several external payment service providers, reports an honest status to checkout, and later handles capture, refund, dispute, settlement, and finance reconciliation. The design must never create a second business charge merely because a client, worker, or provider call was retried. A timeout is treated as an unknown outcome rather than as failure, and the internal ledger remains auditable even when provider APIs, webhooks, queues, or databases are impaired.
discovery_questions: Is the first release authorization-only, immediate capture, or both, and which payment methods and currencies are in scope?
What does the caller consider the business operation: one checkout, one order, one payment attempt, or one provider request?
Which outcomes may be synchronous, and may checkout return PENDING while asynchronous confirmation continues?
What peak attempts per second, latency SLO, availability target, retry budget, and maximum backlog recovery time are expected?
Which provider errors are definitely retryable, definitely terminal, or outcome-unknown, and how long does each provider retain idempotency keys?
Do we need multi-provider routing or failover, and under what evidence is it safe to move an unresolved payment to another provider?
What accounting model, settlement cadence, refund workflow, dispute process, retention period, and audit obligations apply?
Which PCI scope, tokenization, encryption, key rotation, regional residency, fraud, and access-control requirements apply?
What ordering is required among authorize, capture, cancel, refund, and chargeback transitions for the same payment?
What is the operational policy when provider state and our state disagree or an outcome remains unknown past the retry window?
functional_requirements: Create a payment attempt for an order and return a durable payment ID and current state before invoking an external provider.
Deduplicate repeated create, capture, cancel, and refund commands using a caller-scoped idempotency key bound to a canonical request fingerprint and operation type.
Execute authorize or charge, capture, cancel, and refund through provider adapters while preserving provider request IDs and classifying terminal, retryable, and unknown outcomes.
Expose GET status so clients can poll a resource that can be PENDING or UNKNOWN instead of converting timeouts into false failures.
Ingest authenticated provider webhooks, deduplicate event IDs, tolerate out-of-order delivery, and advance the payment state only through valid versioned transitions.
Record immutable double-entry ledger postings for money movement and corrections; never edit historical entries in place.
Reconcile internal attempts and ledger totals against provider objects, balance transactions, settlements, fees, refunds, and disputes, producing an exception queue for human review.
Publish payment state changes to downstream order and notification systems without a committed database change losing its event.
non_functional_requirements: Correctness takes priority over immediate availability: on ambiguous writes, return or retain UNKNOWN/PENDING and reconcile rather than risk a duplicate charge.
Use an illustrative p99 create-request latency target below 500 ms for the local durable acceptance path; provider completion may remain asynchronous and is measured separately.
Provide horizontally scalable stateless APIs and partition background work by payment ID so unrelated payments progress independently.
Preserve per-payment command ordering and monotonic versions; no global ordering requirement is claimed.
Encrypt data in transit and at rest, tokenize card data so raw PAN/CVC do not enter the application database, and enforce least-privilege service and operator access.
Retain an immutable audit trail linking order ID, payment ID, attempt ID, idempotency key, provider request/object IDs, event IDs, ledger entries, actor, and correlation ID.
Bound retries by attempt count and deadline, use exponential backoff with jitter, and protect each provider with rate limits, circuit breakers, queues, and isolated worker pools.
Alert on unknown-outcome age, reconciliation breaks, ledger imbalance, webhook lag, retry exhaustion, provider error rate, queue age, and state-transition conflicts.

core_entities.name: Payment
core_entities.purpose: The order-level aggregate containing amount, currency, customer token reference, desired operation, current state, and monotonic version.

core_entities.name: PaymentAttempt
core_entities.purpose: One controlled interaction with a provider, including provider, request ID, idempotency key, request fingerprint, outcome classification, and timestamps.

core_entities.name: IdempotencyRecord
core_entities.purpose: Maps caller, operation, and key to the canonical request hash, durable payment or refund ID, response snapshot, and retention deadline; mismatched reuse is rejected.

core_entities.name: PaymentCommand
core_entities.purpose: A versioned authorize, capture, cancel, or refund intent processed serially for one payment aggregate.

core_entities.name: ProviderEvent
core_entities.purpose: A verified webhook event retained with event ID, object ID, event type, raw-body hash, processing status, and provider creation metadata for deduplication and audit.

core_entities.name: LedgerAccount
core_entities.purpose: A named account such as customer receivable, processor clearing, merchant payable, fee expense, or cash.

core_entities.name: LedgerTransaction
core_entities.purpose: An immutable balanced set of debit and credit entries associated with a business event and reversal chain.

core_entities.name: OutboxEvent
core_entities.purpose: A domain event written in the same database transaction as the payment transition, then relayed at least once to the event bus.

core_entities.name: ReconciliationCase
core_entities.purpose: Tracks a mismatch or unresolved outcome, evidence collected, owner, remediation decision, and closure audit.

api_interface.purpose: Create a payment using Idempotency-Key; persist the aggregate and return paymentId plus PENDING, SUCCEEDED, DECLINED, or UNKNOWN.
Return current state, amount, version, permitted next actions, and a safe client-facing reason without exposing provider secrets.
Request a full or partial capture with an idempotency key and expected payment version.
Cancel an uncaptured authorization through a version-checked idempotent command.
Create a full or partial refund resource; reject cumulative refunds above captured amount.
Return authorized audit and ledger references for finance and support tooling.
Verify the signature over the raw body, durably record and deduplicate the event, enqueue processing, and acknowledge quickly.
Start a bounded reconciliation run for a provider, settlement window, or explicit list of unresolved attempts.

component_flow: 1. Checkout sends POST /v1/payments with an authenticated merchant identity, orderId, amount, currency, payment token, and Idempotency-Key.

2. The Payment API validates authorization and limits, computes a canonical request fingerprint, and in one transaction claims the caller-scoped idempotency key, creates Payment and PaymentAttempt rows, and writes an outbox event. A duplicate with the same fingerprint replays the stored result; a mismatched request receives a conflict.

3. The outbox relay publishes PaymentRequested keyed by paymentId. The command consumer serializes work per payment, checks the expected version, and sends the attempt to the selected provider adapter.

4. The adapter sends a stable provider idempotency key and local paymentId metadata. Definite declines become terminal; retryable pre-execution failures are retried with the same key; timeout, connection loss, and indeterminate 5xx responses become UNKNOWN rather than failed.

5. A successful provider response advances the state using compare-and-set on payment version, records provider IDs, appends balanced ledger entries where money movement is confirmed, and writes PaymentStateChanged to the outbox in the same transaction.

6. Provider webhooks enter a separate authenticated endpoint. The receiver verifies the raw-body signature and freshness, stores the event under a unique provider/eventId constraint, returns 2xx quickly, and lets an asynchronous consumer retrieve canonical provider state when necessary.

7. The webhook consumer applies only valid state-machine transitions. It uses payment version and provider object identity rather than arrival timestamp; duplicates are acknowledged and stale events are retained for audit without reversing newer state.

8. A sweeper queries UNKNOWN, long-PENDING, and webhook-gap attempts. It polls by provider object or request ID, consumes settlement and balance reports, and either converges state automatically or opens a ReconciliationCase.

9. Finance reconciliation compares provider transactions, refunds, disputes, fees, and payouts with immutable ledger postings and internal aggregates; corrections are new compensating entries, never destructive edits.

10. Order, receipt, analytics, and support consumers receive at-least-once outbox events and deduplicate by eventId. Provider-specific queues, pools, and circuit breakers prevent one provider outage from exhausting the entire payment service.
tradeoffs: Synchronous provider calls simplify checkout but couple latency and availability to the provider; durable asynchronous acceptance allows honest PENDING results but makes the client flow more complex.

A relational database with transactions and unique constraints makes idempotency, state transitions, and ledger invariants easier; partitioning and hot-merchant isolation require more deliberate scaling than a schemaless store.

One active provider per payment avoids double charging during failover; attempting a second provider can improve conversion only after the first outcome is proven terminal or a business-approved compensation process exists.

A double-entry ledger increases storage and implementation effort, but it makes balances, refunds, fees, and corrections independently auditable instead of deriving finance state from mutable payment rows.
Using provider webhooks reduces polling cost and latency, but webhooks are duplicated and unordered; polling and settlement reconciliation remain necessary as correctness backstops.

Long idempotency retention protects delayed retries but increases storage and privacy obligations; retention must cover the maximum client retry and operational recovery window, not simply copy one provider's minimum.
failure_security_challenges: The provider commits a charge but the response is lost. Mark the attempt UNKNOWN, retry only with the same provider key inside its safe window, then query and reconcile; never switch providers blindly.
Two identical client requests race on different API nodes. A unique caller/operation/idempotency-key constraint elects one owner, while the loser waits for or replays the same durable result.
The same key arrives with a different amount, currency, token, or operation. Compare a canonical fingerprint and reject the mismatch rather than silently returning an unrelated result.

A webhook is duplicated, delayed, forged, or arrives out of order. Verify signature and timestamp over the raw body, deduplicate event IDs, authorize only expected event types, and enforce versioned state transitions.

The database commits a payment transition but event publication fails. The transactional outbox keeps the event durable; at-least-once relay and consumer deduplication provide effectively-once business effects within defined boundaries.

A worker crashes after calling the provider but before saving the response. On recovery it reuses the same attempt and provider idempotency key, then retrieves provider state before creating new work.

A malicious or buggy caller attempts amount changes, excessive refunds, or cross-merchant access. Enforce object-level authorization, expected versions, cumulative amount invariants, rate limits, and an append-only operator audit.

Card data or webhook secrets leak. Keep raw card data out of application storage through tokenization, isolate secrets in a managed secret store, rotate with overlap, redact logs, and minimize PCI scope.

One provider degrades and fills shared queues or connections. Use provider-specific bulkheads, bounded queues, circuit breakers, concurrency budgets, and load shedding so healthy providers and read APIs remain available.

Internal totals and provider settlement disagree. Freeze automatic correction beyond a configured materiality threshold, preserve evidence, create a reconciliation case, and use compensating ledger entries after approval.

deep_dives.title: Idempotency contract and unknown outcomes
deep_dives.details: Define idempotency at each side-effecting boundary. The public key is scoped to merchant plus operation, stored before work, bound to a canonical fingerprint, and mapped to the same payment resource and response. The provider adapter derives a stable key from paymentAttemptId and persists it across process restarts. A timeout does not prove failure: the attempt moves to UNKNOWN, retries preserve the key and parameters, and a sweeper retrieves provider state. A new key means a new business operation and is forbidden until the old outcome is resolved or an explicit compensation workflow approves the risk. Local idempotency prevents duplicate admission; provider idempotency prevents duplicate remote effects; webhook event-ID deduplication prevents repeated downstream application. None alone provides end-to-end exactly-once behavior.

deep_dives.title: Payment state machine, ordering, and ledger correctness
deep_dives.details: Model states such as CREATED, PENDING, AUTHORIZED, CAPTURED, DECLINED, CANCELED, PARTIALLY_REFUNDED, REFUNDED, DISPUTED, and UNKNOWN with an explicit transition table. Every command carries expectedVersion; compare-and-set prevents capture and cancel from both winning. Partition commands by paymentId and include sequence/version, but do not claim ordering across unrelated payments. Webhook timestamps are evidence, not the ordering authority. Confirmed financial events append balanced debit and credit postings whose sum is zero in one currency; refunds, disputes, and corrections reference prior postings but create reversals instead of mutation. Periodic invariant checks assert balanced transactions, captured amount not above authorized amount, and refunded amount not above captured amount.

deep_dives.title: Reconciliation as a correctness loop
deep_dives.details: Run three loops: a fast operational sweeper for UNKNOWN and overdue PENDING attempts, a webhook-gap poller for provider objects with missing transitions, and finance reconciliation against provider balance and payout reports. Match using provider object ID, local paymentId metadata, amount, currency, and settlement identifiers. Classify mismatches as missing internal event, missing provider object, amount or currency mismatch, duplicate, fee difference, or timing difference. Safe deterministic repairs can replay an event or advance state; money corrections require append-only ledger entries and, above a threshold, human approval. Track aging and closure evidence so reconciliation is not an unowned batch job.

deep_dives.title: Failure isolation and observability
deep_dives.details: Give each provider its own adapter, queue, worker concurrency pool, timeout policy, retry budget, circuit breaker, and credentials. Keep payment reads and webhook intake separate from outbound call capacity. Propagate correlationId, paymentId, attemptId, providerRequestId, eventId, and ledgerTransactionId, but never sensitive card data. Dashboards distinguish business declines from system failures and show unknown-outcome age, idempotency conflicts, webhook delay, outbox lag, provider latency, circuit state, reconciliation breaks, ledger imbalance, and queue recovery time.

implementation_plan.action: Define the payment state machine, idempotency scopes and retention, outcome taxonomy, accounting entries, provider contracts, threat model, and invariant-based test matrix before choosing infrastructure.

Build one-provider authorization/capture flow with a transactional relational schema, unique idempotency constraints, expected-version transitions, outbox relay, tokenization, secrets management, and traceable status API.

Add signed webhook intake, provider-specific retry workers and bulkheads, UNKNOWN-state recovery, refunds, immutable double-entry ledger postings, and automated operational and settlement reconciliation.

Validate with duplicate and concurrent requests, lost responses, 5xx and timeout ambiguity, crash-after-provider-call, delayed and reordered webhooks, broker and database failover, provider isolation, ledger property tests, reconciliation drills, and controlled rollout.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would make the local payment ID and caller idempotency key durable before contacting a provider. The key is scoped to the merchant and operation, bound to a request hash, and maps every duplicate to the same resource. A transactional outbox publishes a command keyed by payment ID, so authorize, capture, cancel, and refund are ordered per payment and guarded by an expected version. The provider adapter always reuses one provider idempotency key. A timeout or 500 is not a decline; it is UNKNOWN, so we retry safely within the provider window, query provider state, consume signed deduplicated webhooks, and reconcile against balance and payout reports. Confirmed money movement creates immutable balanced ledger entries. Each provider has separate queues, circuits, and worker pools, and downstream consumers deduplicate outbox events. I would test crash points and concurrency with invariants: no duplicate business charge, no invalid state transition, no over-refund, and every ledger transaction balances.

level_expectations.mid_level: Clarifies authorize versus capture, proposes a payment state machine and APIs, uses an idempotency key for mutating calls, applies bounded retries with backoff, handles duplicate webhooks, and identifies that a timeout can leave an unknown outcome. A strong mid-level answer also mentions a transactional database and basic reconciliation.
level_expectations.senior: Defines idempotency scopes and fingerprints across public API, workers, provider calls, and webhooks; refuses unsafe provider failover under ambiguity; models per-payment ordering and concurrent transitions; uses an outbox and immutable double-entry ledger; designs operational plus settlement reconciliation; isolates providers with bulkheads; and explains exactly which transaction boundary is effectively once versus merely at least once.

cases.title: Real-Time Delivery Order Selection and Marketplace Assignment

source_question.title: Design a system to help a delivery driver decide which food orders to pick up, then extend it to how the platform assigns orders at scale.

cases.customer_scenario: A food-delivery marketplace first wants a driver-assist experience that ranks nearby unassigned orders by pickup feasibility, delivery promise, incremental travel, earnings, and compatibility with the driver's current route. It then needs a platform dispatch service that continuously assigns and batches orders across a city while respecting pickup-before-dropoff, restaurant readiness, vehicle capacity, driver eligibility, customer deadlines, fairness, and driver acceptance. GPS updates and order events are delayed, duplicated, and sometimes out of order; the design must avoid double assignment, isolate unhealthy regions, and degrade to safe local heuristics when optimization dependencies fail.
discovery_questions: Is the product advisory, where drivers choose from ranked offers, authoritative, where the platform assigns orders, or a hybrid with offer and acceptance windows?
What is optimized first: on-time delivery, completed orders, driver earnings, travel time, platform cost, fairness, or a weighted objective with hard constraints?
What are the geographic scope, number of active drivers and orders, event rate, dispatch cadence, and lunch or dinner burst profile?
Which constraints are hard, such as pickup-before-dropoff, food compatibility, legal zone, capacity, and deadline, versus soft penalties such as detour or fairness?
How accurate are restaurant preparation estimates, travel-time estimates, and GPS locations, and how should uncertainty affect ranking?
Can multiple orders be batched, what is the maximum active load, and may a route be changed after pickup?
How long is an offer or assignment lease, what constitutes acceptance, and what happens on timeout, rejection, cancellation, or driver disconnect?
What location-update frequency, freshness limit, battery budget, privacy retention, and consent policy are required?
Must assignment decisions be explainable to drivers and operators, and which fairness or anti-gaming rules require audit?
What regional failure behavior is acceptable: stale ranking, manual dispatch, single-order greedy matching, or pausing new commitments?
functional_requirements: Ingest versioned order lifecycle events, restaurant readiness estimates, driver availability, capacity, vehicle and eligibility attributes, and geospatial location updates.
Return a ranked list of feasible orders for one driver with estimated pickup time, incremental distance or duration, promised delivery risk, expected earnings, and concise explanation features.
Create expiring offers or assignment leases and atomically ensure that one order has at most one active winner while one driver remains within route and capacity limits.
Run city-scale dispatch in repeated regional windows, generating feasible driver-order or driver-bundle candidates and optimizing a weighted objective under hard constraints.
Support acceptance, rejection, expiry, cancellation, pickup, and delivery transitions with per-order and per-driver version checks and idempotent commands.
Continuously re-evaluate unassigned orders and available drivers as locations, readiness, traffic, and marketplace supply change without destabilizing committed work.

Provide operator controls for objective weights, regional health, manual overrides, replay, and a full decision audit showing candidates, constraints, score components, model or configuration version, and outcome.
Publish assignment and route updates to driver and customer applications while deduplicating repeated notifications.
non_functional_requirements: Use illustrative targets of under 300 ms p95 for a single-driver recommendation from precomputed candidates and under 2 seconds for a regional dispatch cycle; validate these against market size and optimization quality.
Scale horizontally by market and geospatial cell, with explicit controls for boundary candidates and hot downtown cells.
Preserve ordering per order and per driver through monotonic versions or serial ownership; no global event ordering is required.
Remain useful during partial failure by falling back from global or regional optimization to bounded greedy matching based on fresh local data, while refusing assignments based on unsafe stale state.
Treat driver location as sensitive data: encrypt it, minimize retention and precision by use case, enforce purpose-based access, and audit operator queries.
Support at-least-once event delivery through event IDs, idempotent consumers, transactional outbox publication, and deterministic state transitions.

Detect and alert on stale GPS, dispatch-cycle age, unassigned-order aging, offer expiry, assignment conflicts, optimization timeout, infeasible-rate spikes, cross-cell imbalance, and ETA calibration drift.
Keep regional dispatch failure isolated so one overloaded market, map dependency, or optimizer pool cannot consume the capacity of unrelated regions.

core_entities.name: Order
core_entities.purpose: Contains restaurant and customer locations, ready-time distribution, promised deadline, size, temperature or vehicle requirements, state, and monotonic version.

core_entities.name: Driver
core_entities.purpose: Represents identity, current availability, vehicle and eligibility attributes, capacity, region, last accepted location sequence, and active route version.

core_entities.name: LocationUpdate
core_entities.purpose: A sequenced driver position with device timestamp, server receipt time, accuracy, speed, heading, and geospatial cell; stale or regressing updates do not overwrite fresher state.

core_entities.name: RoutePlan
core_entities.purpose: An ordered list of pickup and dropoff stops with ETAs, loads, constraints, route version, and committed versus mutable segments.

core_entities.name: Candidate
core_entities.purpose: A feasible driver-order or driver-bundle edge with hard-constraint result, score components, incremental route cost, risk, and feature freshness.

core_entities.name: DispatchWindow
core_entities.purpose: A bounded regional optimization snapshot with input watermark, objective configuration, solver deadline, solution, and quality metrics.

core_entities.name: Offer
core_entities.purpose: An expiring proposal tying a driver to an order or bundle with state, lease token, expected order and route versions, and acceptance deadline.

core_entities.name: Assignment
core_entities.purpose: The durable winning commitment connecting driver, order or bundle, route version, decision reason, and lifecycle state.

core_entities.name: DispatchEvent
core_entities.purpose: An immutable event carrying eventId, aggregateId, aggregateVersion, region, correlation ID, and change payload for replay and audit.

api_interface.purpose: Accept a batched or single sequenced GPS update with accuracy and device time; reject unauthorized, impossible, or stale data.
Set online, paused, or offline state idempotently and publish a versioned availability event.
Return fresh feasible ranked orders with score explanations, offerability, and an input watermark.
Accept an unexpired offer using Idempotency-Key, lease token, and expected route version; atomically commit or return a conflict.
Record rejection idempotently and make eligible orders available to the next dispatch cycle.
Return the committed route and route version for driver navigation and optimistic concurrency.
Trigger or replay one bounded regional optimization cycle at a specified event watermark.
Apply authorized restaurant or courier transitions such as READY, PICKED_UP, CANCELED, or DELIVERED using event ID and expected order version.

component_flow: 1. The driver app sends authenticated LocationUpdate batches with an increasing device sequence. The Location Gateway validates accuracy and plausibility, records raw short-retention telemetry, and updates the latest-location store only when the sequence and freshness checks pass.

2. A geospatial index maps active drivers, unassigned orders, and restaurants to H3-like cells. Candidate retrieval searches the current cell and expanding neighboring rings, then performs exact distance and route checks because the grid is a pruning index rather than proof of feasibility.

3. Order, restaurant, traffic, and driver events enter a durable stream keyed by aggregate ID. Projectors maintain regional materialized views; duplicates are ignored by eventId and aggregateVersion, while detected version gaps trigger replay or source-of-truth refresh.

4. For driver assist, the Candidate Service filters hard constraints, inserts each order or small bundle into the driver's existing route, estimates pickup and delivery ETAs, and ranks feasible options by weighted incremental travel, lateness risk, ready-time wait, earnings, fairness, and confidence.

5. At scale, a Regional Dispatcher takes a short, watermarked snapshot of available drivers and eligible orders, generates a sparse candidate graph from geospatial neighborhoods, and sends feasible edges or bundles to an optimizer with a strict time budget.

6. The optimizer minimizes a cost function or maximizes utility while enforcing one active assignment per order, driver capacity, pickup-before-delivery precedence, eligibility, time windows, and route commitments. It returns the best solution found by the deadline plus skipped or infeasible orders.

7. The Assignment Service does not trust a stale optimization result blindly. For each proposal it atomically checks order version, driver route version, active-offer uniqueness, and capacity, then creates a short-lived Offer or durable Assignment and writes outbox events.

8. The driver accepts with the lease token and Idempotency-Key. A transaction or compare-and-set commits the winning assignment, advances order and route versions, invalidates competing offers, and publishes AssignmentCommitted; duplicate accepts replay the same result.

9. Rejections, expiries, cancellations, disconnects, and material ETA changes requeue only affected aggregates. Already picked-up orders remain hard route commitments; uncommitted stops can be re-optimized with a movement penalty to avoid route thrashing.

10. Regional queues, caches, solver pools, and rate limits form bulkheads. If optimization or maps is degraded, dispatch falls back to fresh cached travel times and a conservative greedy nearest-feasible matcher; if location or version freshness is unsafe, it pauses new assignments rather than guessing.
tradeoffs: Driver choice improves autonomy and can reveal local knowledge, but simultaneous self-selection creates races and cherry-picking; platform assignment improves global efficiency but requires acceptance, fairness, and explainability controls.

Frequent global optimization can improve solution quality, but it increases compute, latency, and churn; short regional windows with frozen commitments trade some optimality for responsiveness and stability.
Fine geospatial cells reduce candidate volume but create boundary misses and hot-cell skew; multi-ring expansion, adaptive resolution, and exact route validation add complexity but protect recall.

A sophisticated mixed-integer or routing solver handles coupled constraints well but may miss real-time deadlines; a sparse candidate graph, warm starts, strict deadline, and greedy fallback provide predictable service at lower optimality.

Very frequent GPS updates improve ETA and assignment quality but consume battery, network, storage, and privacy budget; adaptive frequency based on motion and dispatch state is a practical compromise.

Optimizing only travel time is simple but can starve difficult orders or drivers; adding lateness, priority, earnings, and fairness penalties better reflects marketplace goals but makes weight calibration and explanation harder.
Optimistic version checks scale better than a distributed lock across a city, but some proposed assignments fail at commit time and must return to the next dispatch cycle.
failure_security_challenges: Two dispatch workers propose the same order to different drivers. A unique active-assignment constraint plus order-version compare-and-set permits one winner; losers receive a conflict and replan.

GPS updates are duplicated, delayed, spoofed, or out of order. Authenticate devices, enforce sequence and freshness, retain accuracy, apply impossible-speed checks, and use server receipt time without pretending it fixes all spoofing.

An optimization finishes after orders, routes, or availability changed. Every proposal carries the snapshot watermark and expected aggregate versions; the Assignment Service revalidates hard constraints before commit.

A driver accepts exactly as the offer expires or the order is canceled. The authoritative transaction checks lease expiry and current states, returns one deterministic outcome, and publishes compensating customer or driver notifications if needed.
The event stream redelivers or exposes an aggregate-version gap. Consumers deduplicate event IDs, reject stale versions, buffer or refresh gaps, and never rely on timestamps alone for ordering.

A downtown cell becomes hot while adjacent cells are idle. Split or shard the cell, use adaptive resolution and bounded neighbor fan-out, and move cross-boundary reconciliation to a lightweight regional coordinator.

The map, ETA, or optimizer dependency times out. Circuit breakers and regional bulkheads protect the rest of the system; use freshness-bounded cached travel estimates and greedy matching, or pause unsafe new commitments.

A driver manipulates location or repeatedly rejects low-value work. Keep fraud scoring separate from dispatch correctness, avoid opaque punitive actions, audit features and decisions, and route enforcement through reviewed policy.
One region floods shared queues or solver workers. Partition admission, quotas, queues, caches, and worker pools by region so load shedding there does not block unrelated markets.

A restaurant readiness estimate is wrong and causes cascading lateness. Track calibration, represent readiness as an interval or distribution, penalize low-confidence tight connections, and re-optimize only uncommitted route segments.

deep_dives.title: From driver ranking to city-scale assignment optimization
deep_dives.details: For one driver, generate nearby candidates, remove hard-constraint violations, insert each pickup and dropoff into the current route, and rank by a transparent score. At scale, the decision is coupled: assigning one order consumes both an order and driver capacity. Build a sparse bipartite or hypergraph of drivers to orders or small bundles, then optimize a weighted objective such as lateness penalty plus incremental travel and wait time, with penalties for rejection risk, unfairness, and route changes. Enforce one winner per order, capacity, eligibility, pickup-before-dropoff, time windows, and fixed picked-up stops. Use rolling regional windows, warm starts, and a hard solver deadline. Commit through version checks because the solver's snapshot is stale by construction. Measure on-time rate, completion, travel per delivery, wait, acceptance, fairness, solver latency, commit-conflict rate, and regret against an offline stronger solver.

deep_dives.title: Geospatial updates and candidate retrieval
deep_dives.details: The latest-location path is a high-write projection, not the historical source of truth. Every update carries driverId, sequence, device time, server time, accuracy, and coordinates. Only increasing sequences update the projection; stale data remains observable but cannot move the driver backward. Index locations and orders into hierarchical cells, query the current cell plus expanding rings until enough candidates or a maximum radius is reached, and always run exact distance and route feasibility afterward. Select resolution from density and query budget, split hot cells, and include neighboring regions near boundaries. Adapt update frequency: slower when idle, faster while approaching a stop, but mark locations stale after a defined age and withhold new assignments when uncertainty is unsafe.

deep_dives.title: Offer leases, ordering, and race-free commitment
deep_dives.details: An optimizer recommendation is not an assignment. The Assignment Service creates a short lease containing offerId, orderId, driverId, expiresAt, expectedOrderVersion, expectedRouteVersion, and a random lease token. Acceptance is idempotent and atomically verifies token, expiry, order state, driver state, versions, active-assignment uniqueness, and capacity before updating the order and route and writing an outbox event. Events are ordered per order and per driver with aggregate versions, not globally. A duplicate or stale event is acknowledged without reapplication; a gap triggers replay or source refresh. Crossing accept, expiry, and cancellation requests resolve through the same authoritative transition table, producing one committed result and explicit compensation where external notifications raced.

deep_dives.title: Regional failure isolation and graceful degradation
deep_dives.details: Partition the control plane by market or region, with separate input quotas, streams, materialized views, dispatch queues, optimizer pools, caches, and circuit breakers. A small coordinator handles only border candidates so it cannot become the citywide hot path. The normal mode uses current ETA and optimization; degraded mode uses freshness-bounded cached travel matrices and greedy nearest-feasible assignment; safety-stop mode issues no new assignments when order, route, or location versions are too stale. Existing drivers keep their last committed route offline, and state changes reconcile on reconnect. Run fault drills for optimizer timeout, stream lag, map outage, hot cell, regional failover, and duplicate accept, and track both business quality and recovery time.

implementation_plan.action: Define order and driver state machines, hard versus soft constraints, objective and fairness metrics, location freshness policy, offer lease semantics, privacy controls, and an offline replay dataset with baseline heuristics.

Ship driver-assist ranking for one market using sequenced GPS ingestion, hierarchical-cell candidate retrieval, exact route insertion, transparent scores, versioned events, and shadow-mode quality measurement.

Add regional rolling dispatch with sparse candidate graphs, bounded optimizer deadlines, atomic offer and assignment commits, outbox notifications, acceptance and expiry handling, and conservative greedy fallback.

Scale through adaptive cells and regional bulkheads; test duplicate and reordered events, stale GPS, simultaneous accepts, cancellation races, hot cells, stream and map outages, solver timeout, regional isolation, privacy retention, fairness, and offline-versus-online outcome metrics before wider rollout.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would start with a driver-specific ranker: index active drivers and orders by hierarchical geo cell, fetch neighboring candidates, then run exact route insertion and filter hard constraints such as capacity, eligibility, pickup-before-dropoff, and delivery windows. The score combines incremental travel, restaurant wait, lateness risk, earnings, fairness, and confidence. At city scale I would form short regional snapshots, build a sparse driver-to-order or bundle graph, and run a deadline-bounded optimizer. Its result is only a proposal: an Assignment Service atomically checks order and route versions and creates an expiring offer. Acceptance is idempotent and one unique assignment wins. Events are ordered per order and driver, GPS updates carry sequences, and stale solver results fail safely. Regions have separate queues and solver pools; if maps or optimization fails, fresh cached estimates and a conservative greedy matcher keep service running, while unsafe stale state pauses new assignments.

level_expectations.mid_level: Defines driver, order, location, offer, and assignment entities; proposes a nearby-order query and ranking score; handles acceptance and expiry; recognizes duplicate assignment races; and partitions by geography with basic monitoring and fallbacks.
level_expectations.senior: Separates candidate generation, optimization, and authoritative commit; models sparse regional assignment with hard and soft constraints; handles bundles, snapshot staleness, per-aggregate ordering, sequenced GPS, hot-cell and boundary behavior, lease races, fairness, privacy, and regional failure isolation; and proposes offline replay plus online marketplace metrics to tune the objective.

cases.title: Predictive Maintenance Sensor Analytics Platform

source_question.title: Design a pipeline that ingests terabytes of sensor data in mixed formats like JSON, CSV, and XML, then surfaces failure predictions to a non-technical end-user.

cases.customer_scenario: A multi-site manufacturer receives terabytes of vibration, temperature, pressure, and controller data each day from modern connected equipment and older gateways. Payloads arrive as JSON events, CSV batches, and XML files. Reliability engineers need a trustworthy predictive-maintenance platform, while plant supervisors need a simple application that says which asset is at risk, why, how urgent the risk is, and what action to take without requiring them to understand schemas, KQL, or machine-learning scores.
discovery_questions: Which decisions should a prediction drive: inspection, work-order creation, controlled shutdown, or only investigation?
What asset types, sites, device protocols, message rates, batch sizes, event-time delays, and daily data volumes define the workload?
Which feeds are streaming versus file-based, and who owns the JSON, CSV, and XML schemas and their version history?
How far in advance must each failure mode be predicted, and what false-positive and false-negative costs are acceptable?
Is labeled failure and maintenance history available, and can it be joined reliably to asset and sensor identifiers?
Must processing continue at the edge during a network outage, and how long can a site buffer data locally?
Which users may see each site or asset, and can anyone acknowledge, suppress, or convert an alert into a work order?
What retention, residency, deletion, audit, and model-explainability obligations apply?
What are the freshness, availability, dashboard latency, backlog-recovery, and disaster-recovery targets?
functional_requirements: Accept continuous device telemetry and large JSON, CSV, and XML files while preserving the original payload for replay and audit.
Validate envelopes, detect format and schema version, quarantine malformed records, and normalize valid readings into a canonical event model.
Deduplicate retried events, handle late and out-of-order data by asset and sensor, and retain lineage from each normalized reading to its raw source.
Compute windowed features and score assets for known failure modes in near real time, while supporting historical backfills and model retraining.
Present an asset-centric risk queue with severity, confidence, contributing signals, trend context, and an operator-readable recommended action.
Let authorized users acknowledge, assign, suppress with a reason, and create or link a maintenance work order from a prediction.
Capture prediction outcomes and maintenance dispositions as feedback for evaluation and future model versions.
non_functional_requirements: Scale to an illustrative multi-terabyte daily workload and absorb short bursts without dropping accepted data.
Target an illustrative five-minute p95 from accepted streaming event to visible prediction; expose batch-file freshness separately.
Provide at-least-once transport with deterministic event IDs and idempotent downstream effects rather than claiming end-to-end exactly-once processing.
Keep the operator read path available during ingestion or training failures and show the age of the latest evidence.
Encrypt data in transit and at rest, use managed identities and least-privilege site-scoped authorization, and keep secrets out of code.
Support schema evolution, versioned transformations, model rollback, reproducible backfills, and immutable audit records.
Monitor ingestion lag, malformed and duplicate rates, feature freshness, score latency, model drift, alert precision, and work-order outcomes.
Meet customer-defined recovery objectives through raw-data durability, replayable streams, infrastructure as code, and tested restore procedures.

core_entities.name: Asset
core_entities.purpose: Represents a machine or subsystem, including site, type, criticality, ownership, and expected sensor configuration.

core_entities.name: SensorReading
core_entities.purpose: Canonical event containing eventId, assetId, sensorId, eventTime, ingestTime, measurement, unit, quality, schemaVersion, and raw lineage.

core_entities.name: RawObject
core_entities.purpose: Immutable source payload or file plus content hash, format, source, arrival time, and retention metadata for replay and audit.

core_entities.name: FeatureSnapshot
core_entities.purpose: Versioned event-time features for one asset and scoring window, linked to the contributing readings.

core_entities.name: ModelVersion
core_entities.purpose: Identifies training data, feature definition, artifact, threshold policy, validation results, approval state, and deployment interval.

core_entities.name: FailurePrediction
core_entities.purpose: Stores asset, failure mode, probability, severity, horizon, evidence window, explanation, model version, status, and expiry.

core_entities.name: OperatorDisposition
core_entities.purpose: Records acknowledgement, assignment, suppression, work-order link, observed outcome, actor, and timestamps.

api_interface.purpose: Initiate an authorized resumable upload and return an uploadId plus scoped destination for a JSON, CSV, or XML batch.
Return validation, quarantine, normalization, and completion counts without making the client poll internal pipeline components.
Return the authorized, paginated operator risk queue with freshness and human-readable evidence.
Return one prediction, its trend context, explanation, model version, and linked maintenance history.
Idempotently acknowledge, assign, suppress, or link a work order using an Idempotency-Key and the caller identity from trusted claims.

component_flow: Devices authenticate to Azure IoT Hub and publish small telemetry envelopes with stable eventId, assetId, sensorId, schemaVersion, eventTime, and content type; intermittently connected gateways buffer locally.
Large or compressed batches use IoT Hub file upload or a protected ingestion API to land in Azure Data Lake Storage, while upload completion triggers asynchronous processing.

IoT Hub message routing sends telemetry to Event Hubs for independently scalable consumers and routes a durable raw copy to storage; Event Hubs Capture supplies an additional replayable lake path where appropriate.

A stream and file normalization layer detects JSON, CSV, or XML, validates the registered schema, converts units, adds asset context, and writes invalid records with reason codes to a quarantine zone.
Valid canonical readings are written to Azure Data Explorer for time-series analysis and to partitioned lake tables for long-term history, training, and deterministic replay.
A feature processor uses event-time windows and watermarks, updates versioned feature snapshots, and treats late readings according to an explicit correction policy.

An online scoring service loads an approved model version, emits a FailurePrediction with explanation and evidence references, and upserts it idempotently by asset, failure mode, model version, and window.
The operator API joins predictions with asset metadata and disposition state, enforces site-scoped authorization, and exposes a simple risk queue rather than raw telemetry queries.

A web application renders severity, confidence, trend, evidence age, and recommended next step; operator actions call a transactional disposition endpoint and optionally invoke a maintenance-system adapter.

Monitoring correlates eventId, uploadId, featureSnapshotId, predictionId, and workOrderId; outcome feedback feeds offline evaluation, drift review, and controlled retraining rather than automatically changing production behavior.
tradeoffs: Normalizing into one canonical schema simplifies analytics and model features, but every source-specific transformation must be versioned and maintained as devices evolve.
Streaming scores reduce time to action, while micro-batches lower cost and improve throughput; use streaming only for failure modes whose business horizon justifies the operational complexity.

A separate time-series serving store such as Azure Data Explorer supports fast telemetry exploration, but duplicates data already held in the lake and requires reconciliation and retention discipline.
Cloud processing centralizes governance and model operations, while edge processing tolerates disconnection and can react faster; edge inference adds fleet rollout, hardware, and version-skew risks.
At-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers is practical and replayable, but requires durable event identities and deduplication at every side-effect boundary.

Aggressive prediction thresholds find more impending failures but create alert fatigue; conservative thresholds miss events, so the policy should be selected per failure mode from measured operational cost.
failure_security_challenges: A device or gateway retries after an ambiguous timeout, producing duplicate readings and duplicate work orders unless event and disposition operations are idempotent.
Clock skew, delayed uploads, and out-of-order telemetry corrupt rolling features unless event time, ingest time, watermarks, and correction rules are distinct.
A producer changes an XML namespace, CSV column order, unit, or JSON field type without notice; silent coercion would be worse than quarantining and alerting.
A hot asset, site, or partition overwhelms one Event Hubs partition or stream worker while aggregate capacity appears healthy.
The model service or feature store is unavailable; the UI must retain the last prediction with its age and avoid presenting stale risk as current.
Training-serving skew, model drift, or a bad rollout changes alert volume; shadow evaluation, canaries, versioned features, and fast rollback are required.
A compromised device sends plausible but malicious telemetry; per-device identity, rate limits, plausibility checks, anomaly monitoring, and revocation limit blast radius.
A cross-site authorization defect exposes operational data or lets the wrong user suppress a critical alert; authorization must be enforced server-side from trusted identity claims and audited.
Raw payloads or diagnostics contain sensitive operational data; private connectivity, encryption, retention limits, redaction, and least-privilege access are defense in depth.

deep_dives.title: Mixed-format ingestion, schema evolution, and replay
deep_dives.details: Keep the immutable raw zone separate from canonical data. Assign each message or file a content hash and source lineage before parsing. Resolve a schema by source and schemaVersion, validate strictly, and route failures to quarantine with machine-readable reason codes. Transform into a canonical SensorReading with explicit units and both eventTime and ingestTime. Reprocessing writes a new transformationVersion rather than mutating history, and idempotent merge keys prevent a backfill from duplicating serving data. This turns malformed input and schema changes into observable workflows instead of silent corruption.

deep_dives.title: Event-time correctness and scalable feature computation
deep_dives.details: Partition primarily by a stable hash of assetId so one asset's sequence reaches the same processing lane without implying global ordering. Compute rolling statistics by event time, set watermarks from measured lateness, and define whether very late readings correct a prior feature snapshot or only affect offline training. Persist checkpoints and feature definitions. Backpressure should increase lag rather than drop accepted events, and operators should see lag by source and partition so a hot key is not hidden by fleet averages.

deep_dives.title: Prediction lifecycle and non-technical user experience
deep_dives.details: A probability alone is not actionable. Map score, asset criticality, failure horizon, and business cost into a versioned severity policy. Show the asset, predicted failure mode, time horizon, confidence band, top contributing signals, recent trend, evidence freshness, and one recommended next action. Use explicit states such as open, acknowledged, assigned, suppressed, resolved, and expired. Record every transition and make work-order creation idempotent so an uncertain downstream timeout cannot create duplicate maintenance jobs.

deep_dives.title: Model evaluation, rollout, and feedback
deep_dives.details: Create time-based training and holdout sets to avoid future leakage, evaluate precision and recall per asset class and failure horizon, and translate errors into avoided downtime and unnecessary inspections. Compare a simple rules baseline before adding a complex model. Register feature and model versions, shadow-score historical and live traffic, canary by site, monitor drift and alert-volume shifts, and retain a one-click rollback. Operator dispositions are useful labels but can be biased or incomplete, so they require review before retraining.

implementation_plan.action: Run discovery on one site and one costly failure mode; inventory sources and schemas, define the canonical event and asset identity, quantify error costs, and build a labeled evaluation set plus a rules baseline.

Build the thin ingestion slice from IoT Hub and one batch upload through raw storage, validation, quarantine, canonical storage, lineage, replay, and lag dashboards; prove duplicate, malformed, late, and burst behavior.
Add versioned event-time features, offline training, model registry, shadow scoring, the prediction lifecycle API, and an operator prototype tested with plant supervisors.

Canary one production line with human confirmation, integrate idempotent work-order creation, measure business and model outcomes, run outage and backfill drills, then scale by reusable site adapters and capacity tests.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would separate durable ingestion, canonical processing, prediction, and the operator experience. Small authenticated telemetry enters IoT Hub and large JSON, CSV, or XML batches land in Data Lake Storage. Every payload first goes to an immutable raw zone. A versioned parser validates schema, quarantines bad records, normalizes units, and produces canonical readings with stable event IDs, event time, ingest time, and lineage. Event Hubs decouples consumers; Azure Data Explorer serves recent time-series analysis, while the lake supports replay and training. Event-time processors build versioned features and an approved model emits idempotent failure predictions. The UI shows an asset risk queue, evidence freshness, contributing signals, and a recommended action—not raw model scores. I would design for duplicates, late data, schema drift, hot partitions, model rollback, and site-scoped authorization, then launch one failure mode in shadow and canary modes before automating maintenance actions.

level_expectations.mid_level: Clarifies volume, latency, formats, failure horizon, and user needs; separates streaming from batch ingestion; proposes raw storage, parsing and validation, a queue or stream, canonical storage, model scoring, and a usable dashboard; discusses retries, malformed data, monitoring, and basic access control.
level_expectations.senior: Quantifies business error costs and SLOs; distinguishes event time from ingest time; designs stable IDs, idempotency, quarantine, lineage, replay, schema and feature versioning, hot-partition handling, backpressure, stale-data UX, model rollout and rollback, authorization boundaries, and a phased delivery and evaluation plan tied to avoided downtime.

IoT Hub file upload provides a per-upload SAS URI for associated Blob Storage and can notify backend services after a device completes an upload. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/iot-hub/iot-hub-devguide-file-upload

Event Hubs Capture can automatically write streaming data to Blob Storage or Data Lake Storage on time or size intervals, and Event Hubs uses independently consumed partitions as a durable time-retention buffer. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/event-hubs/event-hubs-capture-overview

cases.title: ChatGPT-Accessible Semantic Product Search

source_question.title: Build a semantic search system over Amazon products so ChatGPT could access it.

cases.customer_scenario: A commerce platform has an Amazon-scale product catalog with titles, descriptions, categories, attributes, images, offers, and frequent availability changes. It wants a semantic product-search service that handles natural-language intent such as 'quiet mechanical keyboard for a shared office under $120,' still respects exact brands and model numbers, and can be called safely by ChatGPT through a narrow tool interface that returns grounded, structured product evidence rather than letting the model invent catalog facts.
discovery_questions: What is the corpus size, locale count, update rate, query rate, traffic shape, and required index freshness?
Which source is authoritative for product content, price, inventory, seller, eligibility, and compliance state?
What query intents matter most: exact SKU or ASIN lookup, category browse, attribute constraints, substitutes, compatibility, or open-ended discovery?
Which fields may be embedded, keyword searched, filtered, faceted, sorted, or returned to ChatGPT?
Should the tool return products only, or may ChatGPT compare, summarize, or recommend them, and what evidence must accompany those claims?
How are variants, parent-child listings, duplicate sellers, regional offers, adult or restricted products, and deleted listings represented?
What offline relevance labels, click and conversion feedback, human judgments, and adversarial queries are available?
What p95 latency, availability, freshness, recall, cost, data-residency, and abuse-prevention targets apply?
Is personalization permitted, and if so which user attributes and consent rules may influence retrieval?
functional_requirements: Continuously ingest product and offer changes, validate them, enrich searchable text, generate versioned embeddings, and upsert or delete search documents idempotently.
Support exact identifier and keyword search, semantic vector similarity, hybrid fusion, metadata filters, facets, and deterministic sort options.
Return structured products with ASIN, title, canonical URL, selected attributes, current offer snapshot, availability timestamp, and match evidence; never return raw vectors to the model.
Expose a narrow authenticated search tool that ChatGPT can call with typed query, filter, pagination, locale, and result-limit parameters.
Fetch authoritative live details for a selected product when price or availability freshness must be stronger than the search index can guarantee.
Capture anonymized query, retrieval, tool, latency, and outcome signals for relevance evaluation without silently using sensitive conversation content.
Support zero-downtime schema and embedding migrations through versioned indexes and controlled alias or application routing.
non_functional_requirements: Meet an illustrative p95 search-service latency below 500 ms excluding ChatGPT generation, and publish separate latency budgets for embedding, retrieval, reranking, and live hydration.
Keep product changes searchable within an illustrative five minutes while displaying the timestamp of price and availability evidence.
Scale query and indexing capacity independently and degrade to lexical search or cached popular queries when embedding or reranking dependencies fail.
Measure Recall@K, NDCG@K, MRR, exact-identifier success, filter correctness, zero-result rate, latency, freshness, and cost on representative query slices.
Use TLS, Microsoft Entra ID or workload identity, least-privilege data-plane roles, private connectivity where required, rate limits, and auditable tool calls.
Prevent cross-market, restricted-product, and policy-filter leakage by applying deterministic filters outside the language model.
Make index builds reproducible, support deletion propagation and rollback, and reconcile source counts and sampled records after every migration.
Bound result and prompt sizes so a malicious query or catalog document cannot cause unbounded model, embedding, or search cost.

core_entities.name: Product
core_entities.purpose: Authoritative catalog identity with ASIN, parent and variant relationships, title, description, brand, category, attributes, locale, and lifecycle state.

core_entities.name: Offer
core_entities.purpose: Volatile seller, market, price, currency, availability, fulfillment, and observedAt data that may require fresher retrieval than descriptive content.

core_entities.name: SearchDocument
core_entities.purpose: Denormalized, indexable product projection containing human-readable fields, filterable metadata, facets, source version, and one or more vectors.

core_entities.name: EmbeddingVersion
core_entities.purpose: Tracks model, dimensions, preprocessing template, language, creation time, and compatible vector profile so index and query vectors stay aligned.

core_entities.name: SearchRequest
core_entities.purpose: Typed query contract with text, locale, filters, sort, top, cursor, caller, and correlation ID.

core_entities.name: SearchResult
core_entities.purpose: Grounded product result with stable identifier, selected evidence fields, scores, freshness, and canonical product URL.

core_entities.name: RelevanceFeedback
core_entities.purpose: Privacy-reviewed impression, click, selection, purchase, or human judgment linked to query and index versions for evaluation.

api_interface.purpose: ChatGPT-facing tool endpoint for typed hybrid search with explicit filters, locale, top, cursor, and response field limits.
Return authoritative product details and a fresh offer snapshot before ChatGPT makes price or availability claims.
Internal idempotent endpoint or consumer contract for versioned product upserts and deletes from the catalog change stream.
Record privacy-reviewed impressions, selections, and explicit judgments tied to queryId, result rank, and indexVersion.
Expose dependency-aware readiness including active index version, ingestion lag, and degraded retrieval mode without leaking secrets.

component_flow: The authoritative catalog emits versioned product upsert and delete events to a durable change stream; a periodic reconciliation job detects missed or divergent records.

An enrichment worker validates product state, normalizes attributes and units, derives searchable text from title, description, category, and structured attributes, and keeps volatile offers logically separate.
The embedding service generates vectors with a pinned model and preprocessing template; failures retry with bounds and then enter a replayable dead-letter workflow.
An index writer idempotently projects human-readable, filterable, facetable, sortable, and vector fields into a versioned Azure AI Search index and records source and embedding versions.
ChatGPT invokes the authenticated product-search tool with a natural-language query and explicit filters; the gateway validates allowlisted fields, limits, locale, and policy constraints.

The search service vectorizes the query with the model compatible with the index and sends a hybrid keyword plus vector request, applying deterministic market, availability, category, price, and policy filters.
Azure AI Search runs lexical and vector retrieval, fuses the result sets, and can apply semantic ranking or a product-specific scoring profile to a bounded candidate set.
The gateway deduplicates variants according to product policy, strips raw vectors and internal fields, attaches canonical URLs and freshness timestamps, and returns structured evidence to ChatGPT.

For a selected item or comparison, ChatGPT calls the product-detail endpoint so current price and availability come from the authoritative offer path rather than stale generated text or an old index snapshot.

Telemetry records correlation ID, query class, index and embedding versions, filters, ranks, latency, freshness, tool errors, and privacy-approved outcomes for offline evaluation and controlled relevance experiments.
tradeoffs: Pure vector search handles paraphrases but is weak for exact ASINs, model numbers, and rare terms; hybrid search improves coverage at the cost of more tuning, compute, and score interpretation.
A separate Azure AI Search index scales retrieval independently and provides search-specific features, but duplicates source data and introduces index-freshness and reconciliation work.
Embedding one denormalized product text is simple and cheap, while separate title, description, attribute, and image vectors enable finer retrieval but increase storage and query complexity.
Approximate HNSW retrieval provides low latency at scale but can miss neighbors; exhaustive KNN is useful as a smaller-corpus or evaluation ground truth but is more expensive.

Integrated vectorization reduces custom pipeline code for supported sources, while application-owned embedding gives tighter control over templates, batching, retries, model migration, and multi-source joins.
Hydrating live price and inventory improves truthfulness but adds latency and failure modes; treating indexed offers as snapshots is faster but requires explicit freshness and conservative language.
Semantic reranking can improve natural-language relevance, but it adds usage cost and latency and cannot rescue a relevant product that never entered the candidate set.
failure_security_challenges: The query is embedded with a different model, dimensions, or preprocessing template than the product vectors, silently degrading relevance unless compatibility is versioned and enforced.
Catalog changes arrive out of order or a delete is missed, leaving stale or prohibited products searchable; source versions, tombstones, and reconciliation are required.
A bulk reindex partially succeeds, mixing schemas or embedding versions; build a new index, verify it, switch routing atomically, and retain rollback.
An embedding endpoint, semantic ranker, or search partition is throttled; bounded retries with jitter, backpressure, lexical degradation, and circuit breaking protect latency and cost.
A product title or description contains prompt-injection text; catalog content is untrusted data and must never be treated as tool or policy instructions.
ChatGPT invents price, compatibility, or availability beyond returned fields; the tool contract should require evidence, freshness, canonical URLs, and live detail lookup for volatile claims.
User-controlled filters trigger expensive broad queries or data exfiltration; validate operators and fields, cap top and query size, rate limit callers, and enforce policy filters server-side.
Restricted, adult, recalled, or wrong-market products leak because ranking occurs before an optional model-side filter; eligibility filters must be deterministic and tested at retrieval time.

Clicks and conversations expose personal data or create popularity feedback loops; minimize and aggregate telemetry, apply retention and consent rules, and evaluate quality by query segment rather than optimizing blindly.

deep_dives.title: Index schema and incremental product pipeline
deep_dives.details: Use one stable key per searchable product or variant and preserve catalog sourceVersion. Human-readable title, description, brand, model number, category path, attributes, and canonical URL are retrievable; marketplace, availability state, price bands, category, and policy flags are filterable or facetable; text fields are keyword searchable; vectors are searchable but not returned. Keep exact price and inventory in the authoritative offer service or label indexed values as snapshots. Consume versioned changes idempotently, propagate tombstones, and reconcile counts and sampled hashes. For a schema or embedding migration, build a versioned index, backfill, shadow-query, verify, switch routing, and retain rollback.

deep_dives.title: Hybrid retrieval, ranking, and evaluation
deep_dives.details: Classify exact identifiers before retrieval, but do not rely on classification alone: send keyword and vector components together, apply hard filters, fuse candidates, and optionally rerank. Weight title, brand, model, and category evidence differently from long descriptions; use scoring profiles for business-neutral factors such as availability freshness only when agreed. Build a judged set spanning ASINs, rare model numbers, attribute-heavy requests, vague discovery, compatibility, typos, multilingual queries, zero-result cases, and prohibited products. Compare BM25, vector, hybrid, and hybrid-plus-reranker using Recall@K, NDCG@K, MRR, filter correctness, latency, and cost rather than one aggregate click metric.

deep_dives.title: Safe ChatGPT tool contract and grounding
deep_dives.details: Expose search as a narrow server-side tool, not direct index credentials. The input schema allowlists filters and caps top, text length, and pagination; identity and marketplace policy come from trusted claims rather than model arguments. The response includes only typed fields, canonical product URLs, evidence snippets, and observedAt timestamps. Instruct the model to cite returned products, state when no suitable match exists, and call product details before volatile claims. Treat product copy and user text as untrusted data, isolate them from tool instructions, validate every tool call, and log a correlation ID without storing full sensitive conversations by default.

deep_dives.title: Freshness, resilience, and cost controls
deep_dives.details: Measure catalog-event lag, embedding backlog, index commit lag, delete lag, and result freshness separately. Use bounded embedding batches, backpressure, dead-letter replay, partition-aware capacity, and query caches only where staleness is acceptable. If vectorization is unavailable, degrade to lexical search and disclose reduced mode; if live offer hydration fails, avoid asserting price or stock. Protect cost with request and result limits, cached embeddings for repeated queries where appropriate, vector compression only after recall testing, autoscaling informed by load tests, and budgets by ingestion, query, reranking, and model calls.

implementation_plan.action: Define query intents, source-of-truth and freshness contracts, product and offer identity, policy filters, latency and cost budgets, and a human-judged relevance set with BM25 as the baseline.
Index a representative catalog slice with stable schemas and pinned embeddings; implement upsert, delete, reconciliation, keyword, vector, hybrid, filters, and detailed retrieval telemetry.

Add the authenticated ChatGPT tool and product-detail hydration, enforce typed inputs and grounded outputs, and run relevance, prompt-injection, restricted-product, load, and dependency-failure tests.

Shadow production queries, canary a small caller cohort, compare quality and business guardrails, tune ranking, prove zero-downtime index migration and rollback, then scale capacity from measured traffic.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would keep the catalog as the source of truth and build a versioned search projection. Product changes enter a durable stream, then a worker validates and enriches title, description, brand, category, attributes, and policy metadata, generates embeddings with a pinned model, and idempotently updates Azure AI Search. The index keeps human-readable and filterable fields beside vectors. ChatGPT calls a narrow authenticated product-search tool; the gateway validates filters and limits, then issues hybrid keyword and vector retrieval so exact ASINs and semantic intent both work. Deterministic market, price, availability, and safety filters are applied outside the model. Results return typed evidence, canonical URLs, and freshness timestamps, never raw vectors. Before claiming current price or stock, ChatGPT calls the authoritative product-detail endpoint. I would evaluate Recall@K, NDCG, exact-ID success, filter correctness, latency, freshness, and cost, with lexical fallback, dead-letter replay, versioned index migration, and prompt-injection tests.

level_expectations.mid_level: Explains embeddings and approximate nearest-neighbor search, proposes an ingestion and indexing pipeline, returns product metadata with vector results, exposes a search API to ChatGPT, and discusses updates, basic filters, latency, monitoring, and security.
level_expectations.senior: Separates catalog and offer truth from the search projection; combines exact, lexical, vector, filter, fusion, and reranking behavior; versions embeddings and indexes; designs deletes, reconciliation, live hydration, degradation, zero-downtime migration, evaluation by query slice, prompt-injection boundaries, policy enforcement, privacy, and measurable rollout gates.

cases.provenance_note: The source_backed_facts below are narrow claims verified in official Microsoft Azure AI Search documentation. The Amazon-scale scenario, ChatGPT tool contract, product schema, numeric SLOs, live-offer hydration, policy controls, evaluation set, and rollout mechanics are adapted or proposed additions and are not claims about Amazon or OpenAI production systems.
source_backed_facts: Azure AI Search supports vector fields alongside nonvector fields in the same index and supports both similarity search and hybrid retrieval. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-overview

Azure AI Search hybrid search runs full-text and vector queries in parallel and merges their results with Reciprocal Rank Fusion; the documentation notes keyword search is useful for exact identifiers and specialized terms. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/hybrid-search-overview

Integrated vectorization can use an indexer, a skillset for chunking and embedding, a search index, and a compatible query-time vectorizer; Microsoft states the query vectorizer should match the embedding model used for indexed content. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-integrated-vectorization

Microsoft's vector-search technology guide describes Azure AI Search as a separate managed index suited to multi-source content and search features such as faceting and autocomplete, while warning that a separate index introduces another data copy and source-to-index freshness delay. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/technology-choices/vector-search

Azure AI Search semantic ranker performs secondary ranking over an existing candidate set and does not search the whole corpus again; only the top ranked candidates proceed to semantic ranking. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/semantic-search-overview

The separation of descriptive product search documents from authoritative volatile offers, the typed tool contract, deterministic eligibility filters, and evidence timestamps are proposed grounding and safety controls.

The exact ranking weights, schema, embedding model, index topology, cache policy, and migration process must be selected through a representative benchmark; no official source is claimed to prescribe these case-specific choices.
