cases.title: Design Federated Login Across Stripe's Client-Facing Sites
cases.category: Federated Identity and Cross-Site Single Sign-On

source_question.title: Design a login system for all of Stripe's client facing sites.

cases.customer_scenario: A payments company operates independently deployed customer-facing sites such as a merchant dashboard, support portal, documentation console, and account settings. A user should authenticate once through a central identity domain and enter authorized sites without re-entering credentials, while each site retains its own least-privilege client registration, local session, authorization policy, and failure isolation. This is an interview adaptation and not a claim about Stripe's production architecture.
discovery_questions: Which exact sites and native clients participate, who owns them, and are they on sibling subdomains, unrelated domains, or embedded third-party surfaces?
Do all sites serve the same user populations and organizations, or must the identity layer route workforce, merchant, consumer, partner, and support identities differently?
Does single sign-on mean no credential prompt, no account chooser, or guaranteed access, and which sites require fresh or stronger authentication?
Should signing out of one site sign out that site only or every participating site, and what propagation delay is acceptable?
How are user, organization, role, entitlement, and support-impersonation decisions represented, and which data must each site query live?
What are the peak authorization and callback rates, availability and latency SLOs, regional requirements, and expected identity-provider outage behavior?
How will new sites register redirect URIs, keys, scopes, logout endpoints, owners, and production approvals without creating unsafe wildcard trust?
What browser privacy constraints, third-party-cookie restrictions, mobile deep links, and legacy applications must the design support?
functional_requirements: Provide central authentication and standards-based OpenID Connect authorization-code login for every approved first-party site.
Reuse the central identity-provider session to provide cross-site SSO while issuing audience-specific tokens and creating an independent local session at each site.
Support account and organization selection, MFA or step-up for sensitive sites and actions, and a maximum-authentication-age requirement.
Register each site as a distinct client with exact redirect URIs, allowed scopes, logout endpoint, owners, environments, and key material.
Support site-local logout and a separately explicit global logout that revokes central and local sessions across participating sites.
Propagate account disablement, credential reset, high-risk session revocation, and organization-access changes to relying sites within a defined window.
Provide self-service onboarding and compatibility checks for new sites without allowing a site to mint identities or grant itself scopes.
non_functional_requirements: Target at least 99.99% availability for central authorization and token endpoints and allow already-established site sessions to follow a documented degraded-mode policy.
Complete a warm SSO redirect round trip within a low-hundreds-of-milliseconds regional budget excluding user interaction, while avoiding hidden-iframe dependence.
Isolate a compromised site by using separate client identifiers, exact redirect URIs, audience-restricted tokens, minimal claims, and independent signing credentials.
Validate issuer, audience, signature, expiry, state, nonce, and PKCE at the appropriate component, and protect browser sessions with Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookies and CSRF controls.
Scale authorization, callback, token exchange, discovery, and key distribution independently; cache immutable metadata and keys with safe rollover behavior.
Maintain an auditable registry and change history for clients, redirect URIs, scopes, administrators, consent, keys, and global logout events.
Meet regional privacy and retention requirements and avoid placing sensitive profile or authorization data in broadly readable browser tokens.

core_entities.name: GlobalIdentity
core_entities.purpose: Stable central person identifier and lifecycle state; it is not itself a site's authorization decision.

core_entities.name: OrganizationMembership
core_entities.purpose: Links a person to a merchant or partner organization with status and centrally managed role inputs.

core_entities.name: OIDCClient
core_entities.purpose: Per-site registration containing client ID, exact redirect and logout URIs, allowed flows, scopes, owners, and environment.

core_entities.name: IdentityProviderSession
core_entities.purpose: Central browser authentication state used to satisfy later authorization requests without collecting credentials again.

core_entities.name: AuthorizationTransaction
core_entities.purpose: Short-lived state binding client, redirect URI, state, nonce, PKCE challenge, requested scopes, account, organization, and authentication context.

core_entities.name: AuthorizationGrant
core_entities.purpose: Records user or administrator approval for a client and scope set where consent is applicable.

core_entities.name: SiteSession
core_entities.purpose: Independent relying-site session linked to the central identity, selected organization, assurance level, and central session identifier.

core_entities.name: SigningKey
core_entities.purpose: Versioned token-signing key with key ID, activation, retirement, and publication state.

core_entities.name: RevocationEvent
core_entities.purpose: Durable security signal for global sign-out, account disablement, credential reset, or elevated-risk response.

api_interface.purpose: Publish issuer metadata, endpoint locations, supported capabilities, and signing-key URI.
Authenticate or reuse the central session, validate the client request, gather account or organization context, and issue a one-time authorization code.
Redeem a one-time authorization code with client authentication or PKCE and issue audience-specific tokens.
Publish current and overlapping public signing keys for token validation and rollover.
End the central identity-provider session and initiate configured global sign-out behavior.
Deliver a signed, replay-protected back-channel revocation event to sites that need stronger logout guarantees than browser front-channel callbacks alone.
Create an approved per-site registration through a controlled onboarding workflow with explicit owners and exact URIs.
Version and audit redirect URI, scope, key, owner, or logout-endpoint changes with elevated approval.
Revoke all or selected central sessions for an account and publish downstream security events.

component_flow: A user visits Site A, which finds no valid local session and generates state, nonce, and a PKCE verifier before redirecting the browser to the central identity domain's authorization endpoint.
The authorization service validates the registered client, exact redirect URI, requested scopes, PKCE challenge, and policy before any user interaction.

The identity domain authenticates the user, applies MFA or step-up policy, records the central identity-provider session in a first-party Secure cookie, and asks for account or organization selection when needed.
The authorization service issues a short-lived, one-time code bound to the client, redirect URI, and PKCE challenge, then redirects the browser to Site A's registered callback.
Site A validates returned state and exchanges the code at the token endpoint; it validates the ID token and creates its own opaque, Secure, HttpOnly local session with only the required claims.
The user later visits Site B, which starts its own authorization-code transaction rather than reading Site A's cookie or token.

The browser reaches the central identity domain as a first-party top-level navigation and presents the existing central session; policy may issue a new code without a credential prompt or may require account selection or step-up.
Site B redeems the code for tokens whose audience and scopes are specific to Site B and then creates a separate local session.

For routine requests each site authorizes locally from validated identity context and its own entitlement data; sensitive or recently changed entitlements are checked against the authoritative service.

On global logout, the identity service revokes the central session, invokes registered front-channel logout URLs, and publishes signed back-channel events; each site clears matching local sessions idempotently and acknowledges completion.
tradeoffs: A central identity provider gives consistent security policy and SSO, but it becomes a high-value target and a shared dependency with a wide blast radius.

A shared parent-domain cookie appears simple for sibling sites, but it couples trust, does not work across unrelated domains, enlarges cookie-theft impact, and bypasses per-client protocol controls; OIDC redirects are safer and more general.
Separate client registrations constrain audiences and compromise, but increase onboarding, redirect-URI, key, and configuration management compared with one shared client.
Independent local site sessions improve latency and failure isolation, but immediate global revocation and logout require a separate propagation mechanism.

Front-channel logout is standards-aligned and simple, but depends on browser delivery; signed back-channel revocation improves reliability at the cost of queues, retries, deduplication, and reconciliation.
Rich tokens reduce entitlement lookups, but claims become stale and increase privacy exposure and header size; thin identity tokens plus authoritative authorization checks cost more network calls.

Silent SSO through a top-level redirect works with modern browser privacy controls, but it still causes navigation and cannot promise a prompt-free result when policy, account ambiguity, or consent requires interaction.
failure_security_challenges: An open redirect or loosely matched callback leaks an authorization code to an attacker; require exact registered HTTPS redirect URIs and bind the code to client, redirect URI, one-time use, short TTL, and PKCE.
Login CSRF or response injection binds the victim to the attacker's account; generate and verify state, nonce, transaction cookies, issuer, and PKCE for every authorization attempt.

A compromised low-sensitivity site reuses a token against a high-sensitivity site; each site must reject the wrong audience and accept only its required issuer, client, scopes, and authentication context.
Third-party-cookie blocking breaks hidden-iframe silent authentication; use top-level authorization redirects and treat interaction-required responses as normal rather than looping.

Global logout reaches only some sites because a browser tab closes, a callback fails, or a site is down; use idempotent signed events, retries, session-version checks, and reconciliation in addition to front-channel best effort.

A signing-key rollover causes widespread login failure when validators pin one key or fail to refresh an unknown key; publish overlap, cache by key ID, rate-limit metadata refresh, and test emergency rotation.

The central identity service is unavailable; sites need a deliberate policy for existing local sessions, cached keys, token expiry, sensitive actions, and new logins rather than accidental fail-open behavior.
Account or organization switching leaves stale authorization in a site's local session; bind the selected organization explicitly and force session renewal or live checks on membership changes.

A malicious or abandoned client registration retains broad scopes and redirect URIs; require named owners, least privilege, periodic review, environment separation, and automatic expiry for unused clients.

deep_dives.title: Why OIDC redirects instead of a shared cross-site cookie
deep_dives.details: Each site is an OIDC relying party with its own client registration and local session. The central identity cookie is scoped to the identity domain and is presented only when the browser navigates there. A new site initiates an authorization-code request; the identity provider reuses its own session and returns a code to an exact registered callback. No site needs another site's cookie, and unrelated domains work the same way. Separate clients also permit audience restriction, per-site scopes, assurance policy, ownership, and emergency disablement. A top-level redirect avoids making cross-site SSO depend on third-party cookies.

deep_dives.title: Authorization-code transaction and token validation
deep_dives.details: The site creates high-entropy state, nonce, and a PKCE verifier and stores them in a short-lived transaction record. The identity provider validates the client and exact redirect URI before issuing a code bound to the PKCE challenge. The callback compares state before code exchange; the token endpoint consumes the code once and verifies the client or PKCE proof. The relying party validates ID-token signature, issuer, audience, nonce, expiry, and required authentication context using cached discovery metadata and public keys. Access tokens are accepted only by their intended API, not treated as universal site sessions.

deep_dives.title: Global logout, revocation, and propagation
deep_dives.details: Site-local logout only clears that site's session unless product requirements explicitly request global logout. Global logout first revokes the central session and increments a session or user security version. Front-channel callbacks ask active applications to clear browser sessions, but delivery is not guaranteed. A signed back-channel event keyed by event ID and central session ID adds retries and deduplication; sites reject stale or replayed events and acknowledge processing. Reconciliation compares active site sessions with the current security version. Access remains bounded by local-session and token lifetimes even when a site misses the event.

deep_dives.title: Client onboarding and blast-radius control
deep_dives.details: Treat client registration as production configuration, not an informal database row. A site owner declares exact HTTPS redirect and logout URIs, required scopes, user population, data classification, environment, incident contact, and authentication strength. Automation rejects wildcards and cross-environment callbacks, runs protocol conformance tests, and requires security approval for privileged scopes. Each client has independent credentials and can be disabled without affecting others. Inventory reports stale clients, expiring keys, broad scopes, orphaned owners, and unresponsive logout endpoints.

implementation_plan.action: Inventory sites, domains, users, legacy protocols, authorization sources, logout semantics, assurance levels, browser constraints, SLOs, and migration dependencies; define the trust and threat model.

Implement a standards-based identity domain with discovery, authorization code plus PKCE, token, JWKS, central session, exact redirect validation, key rollover, and one low-risk pilot site's local session.

Add per-site registration automation, organization selection, step-up policy, entitlement integration, site-local and global logout, signed revocation events, audit, and operator controls; migrate sites incrementally.

Run protocol conformance, cross-client audience, redirect, CSRF, replay, cookie, third-party-cookie, key-rollover, partial-logout, entitlement-staleness, regional outage, and compromised-client exercises before enforcing the platform for all sites.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would use a central OIDC identity domain and register every client-facing site as a separate client. Site A redirects with state, nonce, and PKCE; the identity service authenticates the user, sets its own first-party session cookie, and returns a one-time code to an exact callback. Site A exchanges it, validates the ID token, and creates a local opaque session. When the user visits Site B, B starts its own flow. The browser presents the identity-domain session during a top-level redirect, so B can receive its own audience-specific result without sharing A's cookie or token. Each site owns authorization and least-privilege scopes. Global logout revokes the central session and combines front-channel callbacks with signed, idempotent back-channel events because browser delivery is best effort. I would test redirect attacks, cross-client token replay, key rollover, blocked third-party cookies, partial logout, and identity-provider outages.

level_expectations.mid_level: Recognizes OIDC authorization code flow, uses a central identity provider plus per-site local sessions, validates tokens and exact redirects, distinguishes authentication from site authorization, and identifies cookie, CSRF, logout, and availability risks.
level_expectations.senior: Rejects shared-cookie shortcuts, designs separate client and audience boundaries, handles PKCE, state, nonce, key rollover, account and organization context, partial global logout, browser privacy restrictions, revocation propagation, entitlement freshness, client governance, migration, and degraded-mode behavior.

cases.title: Internal Interest Groups and Meetup Coordination Platform

source_question.title: Design a system to help internal company teams arrange events/meetups for hobbies and interests.

cases.customer_scenario: A 25,000-person company spread across offices and time zones wants an employee-only platform where people discover hobby communities, propose one-time or recurring meetups, find a workable time and room, RSVP or join a waitlist, and receive calendar and chat updates. Corporate administrators need moderation, privacy, accessibility, and auditable integration controls without turning the product into a general-purpose social network.
discovery_questions: Who are the primary users: any employee, group organizers, office coordinators, security staff, or HR administrators, and what may each role do?
Is the first release for one office, a global company, or multiple isolated corporate tenants?
Which journey matters most at launch: discovering groups, polling for a time, booking a room, managing RSVPs, or recurring-event operations?
Must the system integrate with Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Slack, Teams, room inventory, or corporate identity, and which one is the source of truth for availability?
Can users expose free/busy windows only, or may organizers see calendar details, attendance history, location, and profile interests?
What are the expected employee count, active-group count, events per day, invitation fan-out, peak reminder volume, and acceptable notification delay?
What policies apply to private groups, sensitive interests, guest attendance, alcohol, cost reimbursement, accessibility, harassment reports, and content retention?
How should capacity, waitlists, no-shows, recurring-series exceptions, cancellations, and organizer departure be handled?
What outcomes define success: event creation completion, RSVP conversion, attendance, repeat participation, cross-team connections, or organizer effort saved?
functional_requirements: Employees can create, search, join, leave, and follow interest groups subject to visibility and membership policy.
Authorized organizers can draft, publish, update, cancel, and clone one-time or recurring meetups with time zone, location, capacity, accessibility, and audience rules.
Invitees can RSVP yes, no, or maybe; full events maintain an ordered waitlist and promote the next eligible person when capacity opens.
Organizers can propose candidate times using privacy-preserving free/busy checks and can reserve a room before publishing.
Publishing or changing an event synchronizes a calendar event and emits chat, email, and in-product notifications without duplicating invitations.
Employees can discover relevant public events by topic, office, time, language, accessibility, and hybrid or in-person format.
Users can report a group or event, and moderators can review, restrict, suspend, or remove content with an audit trail.
Organizers can view aggregate RSVP and attendance metrics while administrators can enforce tenant-wide policies and retention.
non_functional_requirements: Availability and event reads should remain responsive at global-enterprise scale; target p95 under 300 ms for cached discovery reads and under 2 seconds for calendar-backed scheduling operations, excluding provider outages.
Event, RSVP, and waitlist mutations must be idempotent and preserve per-event invariants despite retries, duplicate webhooks, and concurrent updates.
The service must enforce SSO, tenant isolation, least-privilege integration scopes, role-based authorization, encryption in transit and at rest, and auditable administrative actions.
Calendar details are minimized: store normalized free/busy outcomes and provider identifiers rather than copying private event bodies unless explicitly required.
Notification and calendar synchronization are eventually consistent, observable, retryable, and recoverable through dead-letter queues and reconciliation jobs.
The design must support time zones, daylight-saving transitions, localization, accessible venues, screen readers, and reasonable-accommodation metadata.
A regional or provider failure must not corrupt event state; users should see pending synchronization and operators should have replay and repair tooling.

core_entities.name: Employee
core_entities.purpose: Tenant-scoped identity, office, time zone, policy attributes, and minimal profile preferences sourced from corporate identity.

core_entities.name: InterestGroup
core_entities.purpose: Community metadata, visibility, topics, membership policy, owner set, and lifecycle state.

core_entities.name: GroupMembership
core_entities.purpose: Employee-to-group relationship with member, organizer, moderator, or banned role and notification preferences.

core_entities.name: Meetup
core_entities.purpose: Canonical event aggregate containing schedule, recurrence, audience, capacity, location, status, version, and organizer.

core_entities.name: Occurrence
core_entities.purpose: A concrete instance of a recurring meetup so an organizer can change or cancel one occurrence independently.

core_entities.name: RSVP
core_entities.purpose: One employee's response and attendance state for one occurrence, protected by a uniqueness constraint.

core_entities.name: WaitlistEntry
core_entities.purpose: Ordered capacity claim with eligibility, enqueue time, promotion state, and response deadline.

core_entities.name: ExternalCalendarLink
core_entities.purpose: Provider, immutable external event identifier, sync version, last status, and idempotency key without copying unnecessary calendar content.

core_entities.name: NotificationJob
core_entities.purpose: Durable, deduplicated delivery intent for chat, email, calendar, or in-product channels.

core_entities.name: ModerationCase
core_entities.purpose: Report, evidence references, policy decision, actor, timestamps, appeal state, and audit history.

api_interface.purpose: Create a tenant-scoped interest group after authorization and policy checks.
Search visible groups with stable cursor pagination and tenant filters.
Create a draft meetup using an Idempotency-Key header.
Rank candidate time windows from permitted free/busy data without returning calendar details.
Atomically mark the meetup published and enqueue calendar, notification, and search-index work through an outbox.
Upsert the caller's RSVP with an expected event version and return confirmed or waitlisted state.
Release a seat and trigger deterministic waitlist promotion.
Discover authorized upcoming occurrences by indexed filters.
Receive verified provider change notifications, deduplicate them, and enqueue reconciliation.
Create an access-controlled report against a group, meetup, or user.

component_flow: An employee authenticates through corporate SSO; the API gateway validates tenant, identity, rate limits, and request size.
The client queries the discovery service, which combines authorization filters with a search index and returns only groups and occurrences visible to that employee.
An organizer creates a draft meetup; the command service validates group role, policy, recurrence, time zone, capacity, and an idempotency key.
For scheduling, the integration service requests only authorized free/busy windows from the configured calendar provider and the availability service ranks candidate slots.
When the organizer publishes, one database transaction stores the published version and an outbox event so committed meetups cannot silently lose downstream work.
An outbox relay publishes MeetupPublished to a durable topic; independent consumers update search, create the provider calendar event, and prepare notifications.
The calendar adapter writes the provider event using a stable transaction or operation identifier, stores the external mapping, and marks synchronization succeeded or pending.
Invitees submit idempotent RSVP commands; a per-occurrence transaction or serialized partition enforces capacity, confirmed-seat, and unique-RSVP invariants.
If a seat opens, the waitlist worker promotes the earliest eligible entry, gives it a bounded acceptance window, and emits a promotion notification.
Calendar or chat webhooks are signature-checked, acknowledged quickly, deduplicated by provider event identifier, and processed asynchronously.
A reconciliation job compares canonical meetup versions with external mappings and repairs missed, reordered, or expired subscription notifications.
Metrics and traces use tenant, meetup, occurrence, and correlation identifiers while sensitive titles, interests, and calendar bodies are excluded from default telemetry.
tradeoffs: A relational database fits RSVP uniqueness, capacity, waitlist ordering, and moderation transactions; a document store simplifies flexible event metadata but moves more invariant enforcement into application code.

Synchronous calendar creation gives immediate certainty but couples publish latency and availability to the provider; an outbox and asynchronous adapter keep publishing reliable but expose a temporary pending state.
A search index enables fast faceted discovery and ranking but is eventually consistent with the system of record and needs deletion and authorization discipline.
Centralized scheduling across providers creates a uniform product but requires complex OAuth, recurrence, time-zone, and webhook adapters; supporting one provider first is narrower but safer.
A strict first-in-first-out waitlist is explainable; eligibility-aware promotion handles office, accessibility, or group rules but is harder to audit and may feel unfair.
Personalized recommendations may improve participation but require additional behavioral data and governance; explicit topic and office filters preserve privacy and explainability.
Public groups maximize discovery, whereas private or unlisted groups protect sensitive interests but complicate search, invitations, analytics, and moderation.
failure_security_challenges: Two concurrent RSVPs claim the final seat unless capacity and RSVP state are enforced in one transaction or serialized per occurrence.
Duplicate publish requests, webhook retries, or lost acknowledgements create duplicate calendar events or notifications unless every side effect has a stable idempotency key.
Calendar providers can throttle, expire subscriptions, deliver metadata-only notifications, or become unavailable; the UI needs pending state and reconciliation rather than false success.
Recurrence edits and daylight-saving transitions can shift future occurrences or overwrite per-instance exceptions.
An organizer leaving the company can orphan groups, external calendar ownership, room reservations, and moderation duties.
Overbroad calendar, directory, or chat scopes can expose private employee data; adapters need least privilege, token rotation, and tenant-bound authorization.
Sensitive group names, attendance patterns, reports, or accessibility needs can leak through search, logs, analytics, or notifications.
Abusive content, exclusionary events, spam invitations, and retaliation after reporting require rate limits, separation of organizer and moderator powers, audit logs, and appeals.
Out-of-order external updates can overwrite a newer canonical meetup; versions, provider change tokens, and conflict policy must prevent stale writes.
A hot company-wide event can overload one occurrence partition, notification fan-out, and room-booking integrations.

deep_dives.title: RSVP capacity and waitlist correctness
deep_dives.details: Treat one occurrence as the consistency boundary. Keep a unique key on tenant_id, occurrence_id, employee_id and update confirmed_count, RSVP state, and waitlist position in one transaction with an occurrence version. When capacity is reached, create an immutable enqueue sequence rather than computing position from a mutable count. Seat release emits a deduplicated promotion command; only one worker may advance the head, and the promoted user receives a deadline before the next entry is considered. Reconciliation recomputes counts from RSVP rows and alerts on invariant violations.

deep_dives.title: Calendar synchronization without making the provider authoritative
deep_dives.details: The meetup database remains the source of truth. A transactional outbox emits desired calendar state containing meetup_id, canonical version, provider, and operation_id. The adapter retries bounded transient failures, records provider IDs and versions, and never applies an older desired version over a newer one. Webhook notifications are hints: verify and deduplicate them, fetch the changed resource or delta, then resolve organizer edits according to policy. Renew expiring subscriptions and run periodic reconciliation because provider notifications can be delayed, duplicated, metadata-only, or missed.

deep_dives.title: Privacy, authorization, and moderation
deep_dives.details: Derive tenant and employee identity from validated SSO claims, not request parameters. Authorize every search result and object mutation against group visibility, membership, office rules, and role. Request only free/busy calendar permissions where possible; do not persist subjects or attendee lists for unrelated events. Encrypt integration credentials in a managed secret store, redact event titles and reports from telemetry, restrict moderator evidence, and apply retention and legal-hold policy. Log high-impact organizer and moderator actions with actor, target, reason, old version, and new version.

deep_dives.title: Discovery at enterprise scale
deep_dives.details: Write canonical groups and occurrences to the transactional store, then project only searchable, authorized metadata into an index. Partition by tenant and time bucket, precompute upcoming occurrences, and use cursor rather than offset pagination. Start with explicit topic, office, time, format, and accessibility filters. Add recommendations only after defining privacy consent, cold-start behavior, diversity goals, offline relevance metrics, and a way to explain and disable personalization.

implementation_plan.action: Interview employees, organizers, HR, security, facilities, and identity teams; select one calendar/chat ecosystem; define visibility, RSVP, capacity, moderation, retention, and success metrics.
Ship an SSO-protected single-office MVP for groups, one-time meetups, search, transactional RSVPs, capacity, waitlists, and an audit log with no external writes.
Add the transactional outbox, durable workers, calendar and chat adapters, idempotency, webhook verification, dead-letter operations, reconciliation, and pending-sync UX.
Add recurring events, room booking, moderation tooling, global time-zone and accessibility support, load and chaos tests, privacy review, and a measured office-by-office rollout.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would first narrow the launch to group discovery, meetup creation, RSVPs, capacity, and one calendar provider. The canonical meetup and RSVP state lives in a relational database because the hardest invariant is preventing two people from taking the last seat. Publishing commits the event and an outbox row together; workers then update search, create the calendar event, and send chat or email notifications. Those integrations are asynchronous and idempotent, so a provider outage produces a visible pending state rather than a lost meetup or duplicate invite. Calendar webhooks are treated as hints and reconciled against versioned canonical state. Every request is tenant-scoped through SSO, search results are authorization-filtered, and we store free/busy outcomes rather than unrelated calendar details. I would test concurrent RSVPs, duplicate webhooks, recurring-event exceptions, daylight-saving changes, organizer departure, provider throttling, and abuse-report handling before global rollout.

level_expectations.mid_level: Clarifies the core users and MVP, models groups, meetups, RSVPs, and waitlists, proposes reasonable APIs and storage, explains asynchronous notifications, and covers authentication, retries, and basic scaling. A strong mid-level answer traces one publish and RSVP flow end to end and catches the last-seat race.
level_expectations.senior: Defines consistency boundaries and invariants, uses outbox/idempotency/reconciliation deliberately, handles calendar ownership, subscription expiry, recurrence and time-zone edge cases, separates tenant authorization from search ranking, minimizes sensitive data, and ties rollout and observability to explicit product and reliability goals.

cases.title: Event-Driven Engineering Ticket Automation with the Devin API

source_question.title: Build an event-driven automation using the Devin API that solves a engineering workflow problem.

cases.customer_scenario: An engineering organization wants a controlled automation for routine, well-specified bug tickets. When an authorized maintainer applies a devin-ready label, the system validates repository and policy context, creates a Devin session through the organization-scoped v3 API, monitors documented session state, and posts a traceable result back to the ticket. The automation may ask Devin to implement, test, and open a pull request, but the control plane never assumes those outcomes: it verifies structured output and repository state, routes risky or ambiguous work to a human, and never merges or deploys code automatically.
discovery_questions: Which event should trigger work: a label, assignment, CI failure, security alert, support escalation, or scheduled backlog sweep?
Which repositories, branches, ticket types, languages, and data classifications are in scope, and which are prohibited?
What does success mean: a diagnosis, patch, passing tests, pull request, ticket comment, or reduced time-to-triage?
What authority may the Devin session have to read code, write branches, access issue trackers, execute tests, use secrets, or contact external systems?
Which actions require human approval, and can this first version explicitly stop before merge, release, infrastructure, production, or destructive operations?
What event volume, burst size, maximum concurrent sessions, ACU or budget limit, and completion-time target must the system enforce?
How should duplicate labels, redelivered webhooks, edited tickets, cancelled work, session errors, suspended sessions, and waiting-for-user or waiting-for-approval states behave?
Should a new ticket revision update the existing session, cancel it, or create a superseding run, and who owns that decision?
What evidence must be posted back: session URL, branch, pull-request URL, tests, structured summary, failure reason, cost, and audit correlation ID?
What are the provider's documented rate limits and contractual data-handling constraints for this organization, and what must be measured rather than assumed?
functional_requirements: Receive a signed ticket webhook, acknowledge it quickly, normalize it into a versioned work event, and preserve the original event identifier for deduplication.
Authorize the triggering actor, allowlist repository and ticket type, reject incomplete or sensitive work, and require an explicit devin-ready label before session creation.
Create at most one active automation run and Devin session for a ticket revision using a durable idempotency record.
Build a bounded prompt from trusted ticket fields, repository policy, acceptance criteria, playbook, and callback instructions while treating ticket text as untrusted data.
Call the official organization-scoped Devin v3 session API with a least-privilege service-user token and store the returned session identifier and URL.
Monitor the session using documented GET endpoints and state values; handle working, waiting, exit, error, and suspended outcomes without inventing a completion webhook.
Validate any structured output and independently verify claimed pull requests, commits, and CI status through the source-control API before reporting success.
Post an idempotent ticket update with the session link, verified artifacts, tests, disposition, and a human-review requirement; never auto-merge or deploy.
Support operator cancellation, bounded retry, dead-letter inspection, replay, and manual recovery with a complete audit trail.
non_functional_requirements: The ingress path should acknowledge valid webhooks within the provider timeout budget and move durable processing off the request thread.
Delivery is treated as at least once: webhook handling, queue consumers, Devin session creation, source-control writes, and ticket comments must all be idempotent.
The control plane enforces tenant, organization, repository, actor, and ticket policy before spending budget or granting an agent access.
Secrets are held in a managed secret store, never embedded in prompts or logs, rotated, and exposed only to the narrow component or session that needs them.
Global and per-repository concurrency, rate, ACU, and spend limits provide backpressure and prevent a webhook storm from creating unbounded sessions.
Every run carries a correlation ID across webhook event, queue message, ticket revision, automation run, Devin session, repository artifact, and ticket comment.
Transient failures use bounded jittered retries; poison work reaches a dead-letter queue with operator-visible reason and replay controls.
Operational telemetry records state, latency, retries, cost fields when available, and failure class while redacting source code, ticket bodies, credentials, and session messages by default.

core_entities.name: TriggerEvent
core_entities.purpose: Immutable normalized webhook envelope containing provider event ID, ticket revision, actor, repository, event type, and signature-verification result.

core_entities.name: AutomationPolicy
core_entities.purpose: Allowlisted repositories, labels, actor roles, forbidden paths, risk class, playbook, concurrency, budget, and approval rules.

core_entities.name: AutomationRun
core_entities.purpose: State machine and audit aggregate keyed by ticket plus revision, with correlation ID, current state, attempts, timestamps, and terminal disposition.

core_entities.name: DevinSessionRef
core_entities.purpose: Organization ID, Devin session ID, URL, observed status and detail, playbook, creation request hash, and last poll cursor without copying the transcript.

core_entities.name: WorkLease
core_entities.purpose: Durable concurrency and ownership record preventing two workers from creating sessions for the same ticket revision.

core_entities.name: StructuredResult
core_entities.purpose: Schema-validated proposed outcome such as summary, changed paths, tests, pull-request URL, blockers, and requested human action.

core_entities.name: ArtifactVerification
core_entities.purpose: Independent source-control evidence for branch, commit, pull request, test checks, repository identity, and head SHA.

core_entities.name: OutboundUpdate
core_entities.purpose: Idempotent ticket-comment or status intent with target, content hash, attempt count, and delivery result.

core_entities.name: AuditRecord
core_entities.purpose: Append-only record of policy decisions, external calls, state transitions, approvals, retries, operator actions, and redacted outcomes.

api_interface.purpose: Verify the ticket provider signature, deduplicate the event ID, persist the envelope, enqueue work, and return quickly.
Return a redacted state, correlation ID, verified artifacts, and human action required.
Request idempotent cancellation and stop further control-plane side effects.
Allow an authorized operator to retry a recoverable failed or dead-lettered run under the current policy version.
Official Devin API operation used to create a session from a prompt and approved session settings.
Official Devin API operation used to read documented session status and details.
Official Devin API operation used for cursor-paginated session messages when policy permits transcript access.
Official Devin API operation used to send bounded human guidance to an active session when authorized.

component_flow: A maintainer applies the devin-ready label to an eligible ticket; the ticketing platform sends a signed webhook containing an event identifier and ticket revision.
API Management and an Azure Function validate method, signature, timestamp, payload size, tenant, and replay window, persist the raw envelope in restricted storage, and acknowledge promptly.
The ingress function publishes a minimal TriggerEvent to Azure Service Bus using the provider event ID as the message and idempotency key.
A policy worker receives with peek lock, claims the ticket-revision lease, loads trusted repository policy, verifies the triggering actor and label, and rejects forbidden or underspecified work.
The worker creates an AutomationRun and composes a bounded prompt that separates system instructions and acceptance criteria from untrusted ticket text.

A Devin adapter retrieves the service-user credential from Key Vault and calls POST /v3/organizations/{org_id}/sessions with the approved repository, playbook, security, budget, and optional structured-output settings supported for that organization.
The adapter stores only the session ID, URL, request hash, and redacted metadata, then transitions the run to Monitoring before settling the queue message.

Because the documented common flow supports polling, a durable monitor schedules bounded GET requests for session state with backoff and emits state-change events rather than assuming an undocumented completion callback.
Waiting-for-user or waiting-for-approval states notify an authorized maintainer; error, suspended, quota, timeout, or cancellation states become explicit dispositions rather than silent retries.

On a candidate completion, the result worker validates structured output, then queries the source-control provider independently to verify repository, branch, commit, pull request, head SHA, and CI checks.
An outbound worker posts one idempotent ticket comment containing the Devin session URL, verified evidence, unresolved risks, and required human review; it does not merge or deploy.
All transitions emit redacted metrics and correlated audit records; exhausted messages enter the dead-letter queue for inspection, policy correction, and authorized replay.
tradeoffs: Direct Devin session API calls keep policy, idempotency, and audit in the customer control plane; a Devin-native automation can reduce custom code but may provide different trigger and governance behavior that must be validated against current docs and tenant configuration.

Polling the documented GET endpoint is portable and honest about available guarantees but adds latency and API load; an official callback should replace it only if the deployed API explicitly documents and authenticates one.
Service Bus adds durable buffering, dead lettering, and backpressure for high-value work but costs more operationally than invoking Devin directly inside the webhook request.
Structured output makes downstream validation deterministic but can reject otherwise useful free-form results and does not prove that repository side effects occurred.

Passing broad repository or ticket credentials to the session improves autonomy but expands blast radius; a narrow playbook, repository allowlist, scoped identity, and human review reduce flexibility in exchange for safety.
One session per ticket revision simplifies audit and deduplication; sending revisions to an existing session preserves context but creates concurrency, cancellation, and stale-instruction ambiguity.
Automatic pull-request creation saves work but still requires independent artifact and CI verification; restricting the first release to diagnosis-only is safer but produces less end-to-end value.
A central enterprise service user simplifies operations, while per-organization or per-repository identities improve isolation and attribution at the cost of credential and role management.
failure_security_challenges: Webhook spoofing or replay can spend budget and create unauthorized sessions unless signatures, timestamps, actor permissions, and provider event IDs are validated before enqueueing.

At-least-once delivery, worker crashes, and successful-but-unacknowledged API calls can create duplicate sessions; a durable creation record and ticket-revision idempotency state are required because no Devin idempotency guarantee is assumed.
Ticket text is untrusted and may contain prompt injection asking the agent to expose secrets, bypass policy, edit forbidden files, or contact attacker-controlled endpoints.
An overprivileged service user, repository token, session secret, or playbook can turn a routine ticket into cross-repository or production access.
The session may wait for a user or approval, suspend, error, exhaust quota, or exceed the business timeout; each state needs an explicit owner and terminal policy.
A result may claim a pull request or passing tests that do not exist; verify artifacts and checks through the source-control system rather than trusting prose or a URL alone.
Polling can amplify rate limits during a webhook burst; use bounded concurrency, jitter, per-run next-poll time, provider-aware retry, and circuit breakers.
A ticket edited after dispatch can make the running prompt stale; record the revision and either cancel, supersede, or require maintainer review before accepting results.
Secrets or proprietary code can leak into prompts, session messages, queue payloads, logs, ticket comments, or dead-letter metadata without explicit minimization and redaction.
A compromised or hallucinated patch can introduce supply-chain changes, disabled tests, or unsafe infrastructure edits; block prohibited paths and require code-owner and CI approval before merge.
Poison messages can retry indefinitely or disappear into a dead-letter queue with no owner; alert on age and count, preserve reason, and provide controlled replay tooling.
Cancellation can race with completion and outbound commenting; state transitions and side effects must use compare-and-swap or transactional guards.

deep_dives.title: Idempotent session creation under ambiguous failures
deep_dives.details: Use ticket_provider, repository_id, ticket_id, and ticket_revision as a unique business key. In one transaction, create or claim an AutomationRun in CreatingSession state and persist a deterministic request hash before the external call. Only the lease owner may call Devin. If the call returns a session, store its ID and advance state with compare-and-swap. If the network fails after an ambiguous response, do not blindly create another session: quarantine the run for reconciliation using available list or audit data and operator review. Broker duplicate detection is helpful within its window, but consumer idempotency remains authoritative.

deep_dives.title: Safe prompt and authority boundary
deep_dives.details: Build the prompt from typed trusted fields: repository, base branch, acceptance criteria, allowed paths, required tests, prohibited operations, and expected structured schema. Wrap the ticket body as explicitly untrusted context and strip unsupported attachments and links. Give the service user only the documented session permission it needs, bind an approved playbook and security profile where available, and use narrowly scoped secrets. The session may propose or create a branch and pull request if authorized, but it cannot approve, merge, deploy, alter identity, or access production in the first release.

deep_dives.title: State machine and documented Devin semantics
deep_dives.details: Model Received, PolicyRejected, Queued, CreatingSession, Monitoring, HumanInputRequired, Verifying, Reporting, Succeeded, Failed, Cancelled, and DeadLettered. Map documented Devin status and status_detail values into these business states without equating exit with verified success. Poll Get Session at a bounded cadence; optionally read paginated messages only when needed and permitted. A completed-looking session advances to Verifying, where structured output and repository artifacts determine business success. Preserve unknown future status values as Unsupported rather than defaulting to success.

deep_dives.title: Azure event delivery, backpressure, and recovery
deep_dives.details: Use a thin HTTP ingress and a Service Bus queue for high-value commands. Receive with peek lock, complete only after durable state is advanced, and key messages by provider event ID or run ID. Make every consumer idempotent because peek-lock redelivery is possible. Apply global, organization, and repository concurrency gates before Devin calls; delay or defer work instead of spawning unbounded sessions. After bounded retries, dead-letter malformed or persistently failing work with a safe reason, alert on age and depth, and replay only through an authorized tool that re-runs policy checks.

deep_dives.title: Independent outcome verification and success metrics
deep_dives.details: Treat agent output as a claim. Parse it against the requested JSON schema, then use the source-control API to confirm that the pull request belongs to the allowed repository, originates from the expected automation identity, targets the permitted base branch, contains the recorded head SHA, does not touch forbidden paths, and has the required CI checks. Measure trigger-to-session latency, policy rejection, duplicate suppression, session disposition, human intervention, verified-PR rate, CI pass rate, merge rate after review, reverted changes, spend per verified outcome, and queue or dead-letter age.

implementation_plan.action: Select one low-risk repository and ticket type; document current Devin v3 endpoints, organization permissions, status values, source-control webhook verification, policy, budget, success schema, and explicit no-merge boundary.

Build the signed webhook ingress, Service Bus queue, run state machine, unique ticket-revision key, policy evaluator, audit store, redacted status API, and a fake Devin adapter; test duplicate, replay, crash, and race paths first.

Integrate a least-privilege Devin service user, session creation, documented status polling, structured output, Key Vault, source-control artifact verification, idempotent ticket updates, dead-letter handling, and operator cancellation.

Run in shadow and diagnosis-only modes, compare outcomes with humans, load-test bursts and rate limits, red-team ticket prompt injection and secret leakage, then enable pull-request creation for a small allowlist with mandatory human review and rollback metrics.

cases.spoken_answer_60_seconds: I would automate one bounded workflow: a maintainer labels a low-risk bug devin-ready. A signed webhook is acknowledged quickly and placed on Service Bus. A policy worker deduplicates by ticket revision, verifies the actor and repository allowlist, and creates a run before calling the organization-scoped Devin v3 sessions API with a least-privilege service user, approved playbook, bounded prompt, and structured result schema. The control plane stores the returned session ID and monitors the documented status endpoint with backoff; I would not invent a completion webhook guarantee. On completion, structured output is only a claim, so another worker verifies the branch, pull request, changed paths, head SHA, and CI through the source-control API. The ticket receives one idempotent comment with evidence and a human-review requirement. There is no auto-merge or deploy. The hard problems are duplicate session creation after ambiguous failures, prompt injection in tickets, secret scope, rate and budget backpressure, and cancellation races, so those drive the state machine and tests.

level_expectations.mid_level: Chooses a concrete trigger and workflow, verifies webhooks, queues work, calls the documented session API, tracks status, retries safely, stores correlation IDs, and avoids putting secrets in code. A strong mid-level answer includes idempotent ticket comments and a human-review boundary.
level_expectations.senior: Separates the deterministic control plane from the agent, models ambiguous session-creation failures and business state explicitly, uses least-privilege service users and bounded session authority, treats ticket content as prompt-injection input, independently verifies repository outcomes, enforces spend and concurrency backpressure, and never claims undocumented Devin delivery or completion guarantees.

cases.provenance_note: The interview prompt and Cognition AI attribution come from the published Aced question. Devin endpoint paths, permission names, authentication model, documented status fields, pagination, polling examples, and request capabilities in source_backed_facts come from official Devin documentation. Azure delivery statements come from Microsoft Learn. The ticket-label workflow, Azure topology, SLOs, state machine, policy model, prompts, metrics, and no-auto-merge boundary are proposed adaptations, not Devin product guarantees. In particular, this design deliberately polls the documented Get Session API and does not assert that Devin emits a session-completion webhook.
source_backed_facts: The official Devin v3 Create Session endpoint is POST /v3/organizations/{org_id}/sessions and requires UseDevinSessions; its documented request includes prompt and optional repository, playbook, secret, security-profile, ACU-limit, and structured-output fields. Source: https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/sessions/post-organizations-sessions

Devin documents service users as non-human principals for automated integrations and CI/CD, authenticated with bearer credentials whose permissions and organization membership apply to requests. Source: https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/authentication

The official List session messages endpoint is cursor-paginated with first and after parameters, ordered chronologically, and subject to session visibility permissions. Source: https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/sessions/get-organizations-session-messages

Devin's official Common Flows documentation shows polling Get Session and treats exit, error, and suspended as terminal statuses in its example; this supports polling but does not guarantee business success or an outbound completion webhook. Source: https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/common-flows

Microsoft documents that Service Bus peek lock provides at-least-once delivery, that redelivery can create duplicate processing, and that consumers should be idempotent; duplicate detection does not replace receive-side idempotency. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/service-bus-messaging/service-bus-message-loss-and-duplicates

Microsoft's event-driven architecture guidance defines producers, consumers, and channels and notes that decoupling supports independent scalability while asynchronous error handling, ordering, idempotency, and cross-service coordination require explicit design. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/event-driven

The published Aced page identifies the prompt as a Coding interview question associated with the Forward Deployed Engineer role and Cognition AI. Source: https://www.aced.io/questions/7312/build-event-driven-automation-devin-api
adapted_scenario_proposed_additions: The devin-ready ticket-label trigger, low-risk bug scope, pull-request verification, and mandatory no-auto-merge boundary are proposed workflow choices.
API Management, Azure Functions, Service Bus, Key Vault, the run state machine, concurrency leases, dead-letter operations, and polling schedule are proposed customer control-plane components.
The prompt template, structured result schema, independent source-control checks, SLOs, spend limits, metrics, and shadow rollout are proposed safety and operations additions.
